people.name: People
people.text: Adam · Eve · Noah · Abraham (Abram) · Sarah (Sarai) · Hagar · Isaac · Rebekah · Jacob (Israel) · Joseph, son of Jacob · Moses · Miriam · Joshua, son of Nun · Ruth · David · Esther (Hadassah) · Isaiah, son of Amoz · Jesus Christ · Mary, mother of Jesus · John the Baptist · Peter (Simon Peter) · Paul (Saul of Tarsus) · Mary Magdalene · Judith · Judas Maccabeus

adam.name: Adam
adam.text: Creation and human life frame the entry's account of Adam (Genesis 2:7). Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul. Genesis 2:7 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Genesis portrays Adam as the man formed from the ground and placed in Eden to cultivate and keep the garden. He names the animals and receives the woman as his corresponding companion. After both eat the forbidden fruit, their relationship with God and the ground changes: shame, painful labor, mortality, and departure from Eden enter the narrative. Overview sources and context: Genesis 2:7–25 ; Genesis 3:1–24 Verse references: Adam

eve.name: Eve
eve.text: Motherhood and human kinship are the opening focus (Genesis 3:20). The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living. Genesis 3:20 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Eve is the woman whom God forms as a companion for the man in Eden. Genesis describes their shared life before shame, then her encounter with the serpent and their eating of the forbidden fruit. Her name connects her with living humanity. The narrative joins human kinship and mutual belonging with deception, disobedience, painful consequences, and life outside the garden. Overview sources and context: Genesis 2:18–25 ; Genesis 3:1–24 Verse references: Eve

noah.name: Noah
noah.text: The opening verse emphasizes Noah finding divine favor (Genesis 6:8). But Noah found favor in Yahweh’s eyes. Genesis 6:8 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Noah stands within a world that Genesis describes as corrupt and violent. God instructs him to build a great vessel and bring his household, animals, and food into it. The flood narrative makes him a figure of preservation and a new beginning. Afterward, God establishes a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and living creatures, with the rainbow as its sign. Overview sources and context: Genesis 6:5–22 ; Genesis 9:1–17 Verse references: Noah

abraham.name: Abraham (Abram)
abraham.text: The entry follows God's calling and promise of descendants (Genesis 12; 17). Your name will no more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. Genesis 17:5 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) First introduced here as Abram, Abraham answers God’s call to leave his homeland and travel to Canaan with his household. God promises blessing through him to the families of the earth. His later name accompanies a covenant concerning descendants, nations, and land. Sarah’s promised son Isaac becomes central to that covenant, while God also promises to bless Ishmael. Overview sources and context: Genesis 12:1–9 ; Genesis 17:1–22 Verse refere

sarah.name: Sarah (Sarai)
sarah.text: The birth occurs at the promised time, emphasizing fulfillment (Genesis 21:2). Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him. Genesis 21:2 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Sarah, formerly Sarai, is Abraham’s wife and the mother of Isaac. God gives her a new name and promises that nations and kings will come from her. Isaac’s birth in her old age brings laughter into the account. The same household story also records conflict involving Hagar and Ishmael, including Sarah’s demand that they leave so Isaac will inherit. Overview sources and context: Genesis 17:15–21 ; Genesis 21:1–14 Verse references: Sarah (Sarai)

hagar.name: Hagar
hagar.text: God attends to distress and preserves Hagar and her child (Genesis 16; 21). She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?” Genesis 16:13 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Hagar is Sarai’s Egyptian servant and the mother of Abram’s son Ishmael. After harsh treatment, she flees into the wilderness, where God’s messenger addresses her distress and her child’s future. Later, sent away with Ishmael, she faces a desperate shortage of water. God hears the boy and shows her a well, placing survival and divine attention at the center of her story. Overview sources and context: Genesis 16:1–16 ; Genesis 21:8–21 Ver

isaac.name: Isaac
isaac.text: The entry centers on birth, marriage, love and family relationships. Abraham called his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac. Genesis 21:3 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Isaac is the son born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age. He marries Rebekah after Abraham’s servant brings her from his relatives, and the account emphasizes his love for her. Isaac prays when she cannot conceive, and she bears Esau and Jacob. Their differing temperaments and their parents’ different attachments introduce the rivalry of the next generation. Overview sources and context: Genesis 24:59–67 ; Genesis 25:19–34 Verse references: Isaac

rebekah.name: Rebekah
rebekah.text: Marriage, motherhood and family attachments are the entry's focus. Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob. Genesis 25:28 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Rebekah first meets Abraham’s servant at a spring, where she draws water for him and his camels. She agrees to leave her family and becomes Isaac’s wife. During a difficult pregnancy, she seeks God and hears that two peoples are within her. Her sons Esau and Jacob become rivals, and Genesis records her particular attachment to Jacob. Overview sources and context: Genesis 24:10–67 ; Genesis 25:19–34 Verse references: Rebekah

jacob.name: Jacob (Israel)
jacob.text: The encounter and blessing accompany Jacob's new name (Genesis 32). He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.” Genesis 32:28 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Jacob is the younger twin of Esau and the son of Isaac and Rebekah. He acquires Esau’s birthright in exchange for food, beginning a story marked by contested blessing and family tension. Years later, afraid to meet his brother, he prays for deliverance. During a night of wrestling near the Jabbok, he receives the name Israel and leaves with a limp. Overview sources and context: Genesis 25:19–34 ; Genesis 32:1–32 Verse references: Jacob (Israel)

joseph-son-of-jacob.name: Joseph, son of Jacob
joseph-son-of-jacob.text: God's provision preserves Joseph's household and reconciles brothers (Genesis 39; 45). Yahweh was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. He was in the house of his master the Egyptian. Genesis 39:2 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) This Joseph is Jacob’s son, sold into Egypt by his brothers. In Potiphar’s household he prospers, resists his master’s wife, and is imprisoned after her accusation. Later, ruling in Egypt during famine, he reveals himself to his brothers and provides for the family. Joseph interprets his painful displacement through God’s work of preserving life and urges his father to join him. Overview sources and context: Genesis 39:1–23 ; Genesis 45:1–28 Verse references:

moses.name: Moses
moses.text: God calls and commissions Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4). When Yahweh saw that he came over to see, God called to him out of the middle of the bush, and said, “Moses! Moses!” He said, “Here I am.” Exodus 3:4 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Moses encounters God at a burning bush while tending his father-in-law’s flock. He is commissioned to confront Pharaoh and bring Israel out of Egyptian oppression, despite his questions about his own fitness. Deuteronomy remembers his extraordinary signs and his closeness to God. He dies in Moab after seeing the promised land, and Joshua succeeds him as Israel’s leader. Overview sources and context: Exodus 3:1–22 ; Deuteronomy 34:1–12 Verse ref

miriam.name: Miriam
miriam.text: Miriam leads music and praise after the sea crossing (Exodus 15:20–21). Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances. Exodus 15:20 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Miriam is named as a prophetess and Aaron’s sister when she leads the women in music and dancing after Israel’s passage through the sea. Her song celebrates God’s victory over Pharaoh’s forces. Numbers also records her and Aaron challenging Moses’ unique authority. After Miriam is afflicted and Moses prays for her, the community waits until her period outside the camp ends. Overview sources and context: Exodus 15:19–21 ; Numbers

joshua.name: Joshua, son of Nun
joshua.text: Leadership is joined to keeping and applying God's covenant instruction (Joshua 1). So Yahweh was with Joshua; and his fame was in all the land. Joshua 6:27 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Joshua, son of Nun and servant of Moses, receives leadership after Moses’ death. God commissions him to bring Israel across the Jordan and repeatedly connects courage with obedience to the law. At Jericho he directs the procession around the city, its capture, and the rescue of Rahab’s household. His story combines leadership, covenant obedience, warfare, and the settlement of Israel. Overview sources and context: Joshua 1:1–18 ; Joshua 6:1–27 Verse references: Joshua, son of Nun

ruth.name: Ruth
ruth.text: Marriage, loyal family love and the birth of a child frame Ruth's entry. So Boaz took Ruth and she became his wife; and he went in to her, and Yahweh enabled her to conceive, and she bore a son. Ruth 4:13 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Ruth is a Moabite widow who binds her future to Naomi, her bereaved mother-in-law, and travels with her to Bethlehem. Her pledge joins loyalty to Naomi with belonging to Naomi’s people and God. She later marries Boaz and bears Obed. The book closes by connecting this renewed household to Jesse and David, making family faithfulness part of Israel’s royal genealogy. Overview sources and context: Ruth 1:1–22 ; Ruth 4:1–22 Verse references: Ruth

david.name: David
david.text: The opening kingship account includes David's anointing (2 Samuel 5:1–4); his later sin is a separate indigo theme. David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. 2 Samuel 5:4 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) David becomes king over all Israel after ruling in Hebron, captures Jerusalem, and makes its stronghold his city. The narrative connects his growing power with God’s presence. It also exposes grave wrongdoing: Nathan confronts him for taking Uriah’s wife and causing Uriah’s death. David confesses his sin, while the account insists that forgiveness does not remove the consequences for his household. Overview sources and context: 2 Samuel 5:1–12 ; 2 Samu

esther.name: Esther (Hadassah)
esther.text: The overview centers on faithful action for her people's deliverance (Esther 4). The king loved Esther more than all the women, and she obtained favor and kindness in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown on her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. Esther 2:17 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Esther, also called Hadassah, is a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai who becomes queen to Ahasuerus. Initially she conceals her people and family background. When Haman’s decree threatens the Jews, Mordecai urges her to petition the king. She calls for fasting and resolves to approach him without a summons, accepting the danger for the sake of her people

isaiah.name: Isaiah, son of Amoz
isaiah.text: The entry introduces a prophet's vision and commission (Isaiah 1; 6). The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Isaiah 1:1 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Isaiah is introduced as the son of Amoz, whose vision concerns Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of four kings. His book condemns worship joined to injustice and calls for the defense of vulnerable people. In his temple vision, he confesses unclean lips, receives cleansing, and answers God’s summons to speak to a people whose resistance will bring severe judgment. Overview sources and context: Isaiah 1:1–27 ; Isaiah 6:1–13 Ve

jesus-christ.name: Jesus Christ
jesus-christ.text: The entry identifies Jesus as Christ, Son and incarnate Word. The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. John 1:14 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) The New Testament presents Jesus as the Christ and Son of God, the divine Word who becomes flesh. John describes him calling disciples and revealing God’s glory through his presence among people. After his death, the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and the disciples, shows his wounds, and commissions them. His inclusion among people follows the biblical account of incarnation and does not reduce his identity to humanity alone. Overview sources and

mary-mother-of-jesus.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
mary-mother-of-jesus.text: Mary answers God's announcement with commitment: let it be according to your word (Luke 1:38). Mary said, “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” Then the angel departed from her. Luke 1:38 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Mary is the woman of Nazareth to whom Gabriel announces the birth of Jesus through the Holy Spirit. Pledged to Joseph, she receives the message with trust and later praises God’s mercy toward the humble and hungry. Luke describes her giving birth in Bethlehem and pondering the shepherds’ report. This entry concerns Jesus’ mother, distinct from the separately named Mary Magdalene. Overview sources and context: Luke 1:26–56 ; Luke 2

john-the-baptist.name: John the Baptist
john-the-baptist.text: The opening identifies John as sent by God to bear witness (John 1:6). There came a man sent from God, whose name was John. John 1:6 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) John the Baptist, called John the Baptizer in this translation, preaches repentance in the wilderness and baptizes in the Jordan. His austere clothing and food accompany a message that demands changed conduct rather than reliance on ancestry. He baptizes Jesus and points beyond himself to the one who brings the Holy Spirit. John’s Gospel presents him as a witness who directs others toward Jesus. Overview sources and context: Matthew 3:1–17 ; John 1:19–37 Verse references: John the Baptist

peter.name: Peter (Simon Peter)
peter.text: Peter's opening confession identifies Jesus as Christ and Son of God (Matthew 16:16). Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Matthew 16:16 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Simon Peter is a disciple who confesses Jesus as the Christ and Son of God, yet then resists Jesus’ teaching about suffering and receives a sharp rebuke. John places him among the disciples fishing when the risen Jesus appears beside the sea. Jesus questions him about love and entrusts him with caring for his sheep, joining discipleship to responsibility and costly following. Overview sources and context: Matthew 16:13–28 ; John 21:1–22 Verse references: Peter (Simon Peter)

paul.name: Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
paul.text: The overview follows Paul's divine calling and mission to bear witness (Acts 9; 13). Immediately in the synagogues he proclaimed the Christ, that he is the Son of God. Acts 9:20 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Paul, also called Saul, is the man of Tarsus who persecutes Jesus’ followers before encountering Jesus on the road to Damascus. Ananias visits him, his sight returns, and he is baptized. Acts later follows him and Barnabas as they travel, preach Jesus’ resurrection, and address both Jewish and Gentile audiences. The text presents his mission as a divine calling involving witness and suffering. Overview sources and context: Acts 9:1–30 ; Acts 13:1–52 Verse references: Paul (Saul of

mary-magdalene.name: Mary Magdalene
mary-magdalene.text: Mary witnesses and announces the risen Lord (John 20:18). Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her. John 20:18 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Mary Magdalene is named among the women accompanying Jesus, from whom seven demons had gone out. Luke places her within a group of women who supported the ministry from their possessions. In John’s resurrection account, she visits the tomb, weeps at the apparent loss of Jesus’ body, recognizes him when he calls her name, and carries his message to the disciples. Overview sources and context: Luke 8:1–3 ; John 20:1–18 Verse references: Mary Magdalene

judith.name: Judith
judith.text: The overview emphasizes trust and the deliverance of Israel (Judith 8; 13). Deuterocanonical: The source edition identifies Judith as scripture in the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, and Russian Orthodox Churches. Judith was a widow in her house three years and four months. Judith 8:4 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Judith is a devout widow living in Bethulia during a crisis of siege and thirst. She challenges the city’s leaders for imposing a deadline on God’s help and undertakes her own dangerous plan. In Holofernes’ tent she prays for strength, kills the enemy commander, and returns with her maid. The narrative presents her courage and trust as instruments of Israel’s deliverance. Ove

judas-maccabeus.name: Judas Maccabeus
judas-maccabeus.text: The overview culminates in cleansing the sanctuary and restoring worship (1 Maccabees 4). Deuterocanonical: The source edition identifies 1 Maccabees as scripture in the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, and Russian Orthodox Churches. His son Judas, who was called Maccabaeus, rose up in his place. 1 Maccabees 3:1 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Judas Maccabeus, spelled Maccabaeus in this translation, is a son of Mattathias and a military leader of Israel. He takes up leadership after his father and fights to defend his people’s covenantal life. Following victories, he and his companions cleanse the desecrated sanctuary and restore its worship. They establish an annual eight-day celebration

places.name: Places
places.text: Eden · Mountains of Ararat · Ur of the Chaldees · Haran · Canaan · Egypt · Mount Sinai · Jordan River · Jericho · Bethel · Hebron · Bethlehem · Jerusalem · Samaria · Nineveh · Babylon · Nazareth · Galilee · Capernaum · Sea of Galilee · Gethsemane · Golgotha · Antioch in Syria · Ephesus · Rome

eden.name: Eden
eden.text: God's planting and provision of humanity's first garden home introduce this place (Genesis 2). And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed. Genesis 2:8 · King James Version (KJV) Genesis presents Eden as the setting of humanity’s first garden home. God plants its trees, supplies its water, and gives the human a responsibility to cultivate and keep it. The garden becomes the scene of disobedience and expulsion, with access to the tree of life guarded afterward. Its narrative river descriptions do not establish an exact modern location. Overview sources and context: Genesis 2:8–17 ; Genesis 3:1–24 Verse references: Eden

ararat.name: Mountains of Ararat
ararat.text: The ark's resting place belongs to the flood narrative's preservation and deliverance (Genesis 8). And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat. Genesis 8:4 · King James Version (KJV) Ararat enters the flood narrative when Noah’s ark comes to rest as the waters recede. Genesis speaks of mountains in the plural, without identifying one particular summit. Noah subsequently waits, sends birds, leaves the ark, and offers sacrifice; God’s covenant follows. The passage supplies a narrative region of landing, not coordinates or proof that a modern mountain preserves the ark. Overview sources and context: Genesis 8:1–22 ; Genesis 9:8–17 V

ur.name: Ur of the Chaldees
ur.text: God recalls calling Abram out and promising him the land (Genesis 15:7). And he said unto him, I am the LORD that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give thee this land to inherit it. Genesis 15:7 · King James Version (KJV) Ur of the Chaldees is the starting point of Terah’s household journey toward Canaan in Genesis. Abram, Sarai, and Lot travel with Terah, stopping in Haran. Later, God’s covenant speech recalls bringing Abram out of Ur and connects that departure with the promised land. The city functions as a remembered origin in a story of migration, kinship, and divine calling. Overview sources and context: Genesis 11:27–32 ; Genesis 15:1–21 Verse references: Ur of the Chaldees

haran.name: Haran
haran.text: The entry opens with Terah's household, settlement and family history. And the days of Terah were two hundred and five years: and Terah died in Haran. Genesis 11:32 · King James Version (KJV) Haran is the place where Terah’s migrating household settles and where Terah dies. Abram later leaves it for Canaan in response to God’s call, taking Sarai, Lot, and their household. Genesis also names Haran as Jacob’s destination when he leaves Beer-sheba. These journeys make it an important family waypoint; the place should be distinguished from Abram’s brother of the same name. Overview sources and context: Genesis 12:1–5 ; Genesis 28:10–15 Verse references: Haran

canaan.name: Canaan
canaan.text: The entry centers on the land promised to Abram's descendants (Genesis 12; 15). And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came. Genesis 12:5 · King James Version (KJV) Canaan is a land containing numerous peoples and settlements, rather than a single city. Genesis places Abram’s arrival, journeys, and altar building there while acknowledging its existing inhabitants. The promise of land to his descendants develops within the covenant narrative. Reading the surrounding passages keeps the physical landsc

egypt.name: Egypt
egypt.text: The opening quotation emphasizes deliverance from bondage (Exodus 20:2); other Egyptian settings can take different colors. I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Exodus 20:2 · King James Version (KJV) Egypt has more than one role in biblical narrative. Exodus opens with Jacob’s descendants living there, then describes a new king’s oppression and forced labor. Deliverance from that bondage becomes the introduction to the commandments. Matthew later presents Egypt as refuge for the young Jesus and his family from Herod. Its significance depends on each episode, rather than one fixed symbolic meaning. Overview sources and context:

sinai.name: Mount Sinai
sinai.text: Sinai is the setting of the covenant and commandments (Exodus 19–20). And the LORD came down upon mount Sinai, on the top of the mount: and the LORD called Moses up to the top of the mount; and Moses went up. Exodus 19:20 · King James Version (KJV) Sinai is the wilderness mountain before which Israel camps after leaving Egypt. Exodus describes divine descent in fire, smoke, thunder, and trumpet sound, while Moses mediates between God and the people. Boundaries around the mountain dramatize its holiness. The following commandments establish the covenant’s demands. These passages identify the mountain’s narrative role without settling the exact location of a modern summit. Overview sources and

jordan.name: Jordan River
jordan.text: The opening baptism scene marks the beginning of Jesus' public mission (Mark 1:9–11). And it came to pass in those days, that Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee, and was baptized of John in Jordan. Mark 1:9 · King James Version (KJV) The Jordan is a river associated with decisive crossings and beginnings. In Joshua, priests carrying the covenant ark stand in its waters as Israel crosses on dry ground opposite Jericho. In Mark, John baptizes people there, and Jesus comes from Nazareth to be baptized. The accounts give the same physical river distinct roles in Israel’s entry into the land and Jesus’ public story. Overview sources and context: Joshua 3:1–17 ; Mark 1:4–11 Verse references: Jord

jericho.name: Jericho
jericho.text: The opening Gospel context leads to Zacchaeus's salvation (Luke 19:1–10); Joshua's judgment scene has a different emphasis. And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. Luke 19:1 · King James Version (KJV) Jericho appears as a fortified city in Joshua’s account of Israel’s entry into Canaan. Its walls fall after ritual processions and a shout; Rahab’s household is spared amid the destruction. Much later in Luke’s narrative, Jesus passes through Jericho and receives Zacchaeus, whose response includes restitution. These are different episodes and periods, not a claim that every described structure survived unchanged. Overview sources and context: Joshua 6:1–25 ; Luke 19:1–10 Verse references:

bethel.name: Bethel
bethel.text: Jacob's dream and God's promise introduce the place (Genesis 28). And he called the name of that place Beth-el: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first. Genesis 28:19 · King James Version (KJV) Bethel is associated with Jacob’s dream of a ladder reaching heaven and God’s promise of presence and return. Jacob marks the place with a stone pillar, pours oil on it, and names it Bethel, explained as the house of God. In Kings, it becomes a royal sanctuary under Jeroboam, whose calf worship the narrator condemns. Its biblical associations therefore include both revelation and contested worship. Overview sources and context: Genesis 28:10–22 ; 1 Kings 12:25–33 Verse references: Bethel

hebron.name: Hebron
hebron.text: Sarah's death, mourning and the ancestral burial property frame the entry (Genesis 23). And Sarah died in Kirjath-arba; the same is Hebron in the land of Canaan: and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her. Genesis 23:2 · King James Version (KJV) Hebron, also called Kirjath-arba in Genesis, is connected with Sarah’s death and Abraham’s purchase of a burial property at Machpelah. The transaction gives the family a recognized burial place in Canaan. In Samuel, David rules Judah from Hebron before moving to Jerusalem, and Israel’s elders anoint him there. The city thus joins ancestral memory, landholding, mourning, and the beginnings of David’s united kingship. Overview sources and

bethlehem.name: Bethlehem
bethlehem.text: The opening verse identifies the birthplace of Jesus (Matthew 2:1). Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, Matthew 2:1 · King James Version (KJV) Bethlehem in Judah is the town associated with Jesse’s family and Samuel’s anointing of David. Matthew and Luke identify it as Jesus’ birthplace, giving the town a central place in their accounts of his origins. Luke explicitly connects Joseph’s journey there with David’s lineage. These narrative links explain Bethlehem’s importance without turning later buildings or local traditions into details supplied by the verses. Overview sources and context: 1 Sam

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: Psalm 122 introduces the gathered tribes' worship and prayer for the city. Jerusalem is builded as a city that is compact together: Psalm 122:3 · King James Version (KJV) Jerusalem becomes David’s royal city after his capture of the stronghold of Zion. Psalm 122 celebrates its gathered tribes, worship, judgment, and peace. Luke presents Jesus approaching the city, grieving over its future, and teaching in the temple. These passages reveal an inhabited political and religious center whose streets, gates, and sanctuary carry different meanings across successive biblical settings. Overview sources and context: 2 Samuel 5:6–12 ; Luke 19:28–48 Verse references: Jerusalem

samaria.name: Samaria
samaria.text: The entry first identifies a built city, its landscape and inhabitants; this is geography, not a moral judgment on a people. And he bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver, and built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, after the name of Shemer, owner of the hill, Samaria. 1 Kings 16:24 · King James Version (KJV) Samaria names both a city and, in later passages, a wider region. Kings describes Omri building the city on a purchased hill and later recounts its capture by Assyria. John’s Gospel uses Samaria for the region through which Jesus travels, locating his conversation with a Samaritan woman at Sychar. Keeping city and region distinct prevents

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.text: Prophetic warning, repentance and judgment frame the cited Jonah and Nahum accounts. So Jonah arose, and went unto Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceeding great city of three days’ journey. Jonah 3:3 · King James Version (KJV) Nineveh is the great city to which Jonah is sent with a warning. Its people, from ordinary inhabitants to the king, respond with fasting and a call to abandon violence, and the threatened destruction is withheld. Nahum addresses the same named city through fierce imagery of bloodshed, exploitation, and judgment. The two books offer distinct prophetic treatments rather than a single uncomplicated portrait. Overview sources and context: J

babylon.name: Babylon
babylon.text: Conquest, exile and the judgment of corrupt power frame the cited accounts. By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion. Psalm 137:1 · King James Version (KJV) Babylon is associated with imperial conquest and the displacement of Judah. Kings recounts Jerusalem’s destruction and the removal of people and temple objects to Babylon; Psalm 137 voices the grief of exile beside its rivers. Revelation later reuses Babylon in an apocalyptic vision of corrupt wealth and judgment. That visionary use should be distinguished from the physical city and exile setting of earlier narratives. Overview sources and context: 2 Kings 25:1–21 ; Revelation 18:1–24 Verse refer

nazareth.name: Nazareth
nazareth.text: The opening quotation explicitly marks prophetic fulfillment (Matthew 2:23). And he came and dwelt in a city called Nazareth: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, He shall be called a Nazarene. Matthew 2:23 · King James Version (KJV) Nazareth is the Galilean town where the Gospels locate Jesus’ upbringing. Luke describes his return there with his parents and later his reading of Isaiah in its synagogue. The hometown audience’s response moves from wonder to anger as he challenges their expectations. Nazareth therefore supplies both the familiar social setting behind the designation Jesus of Nazareth and a scene of contested recognition. Overview sources and context: Lu

galilee.name: Galilee
galilee.text: The entry follows Jesus' proclamation and teaching ministry in this region. And he preached in their synagogues throughout all Galilee, and cast out devils. Mark 1:39 · King James Version (KJV) Galilee is a region containing towns, villages, and the lake around which much of Jesus’ Gospel ministry unfolds. Matthew locates his move to Capernaum, proclamation, healings, and the calling of fishermen there. In Matthew’s concluding scene, the disciples meet the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee. The region thus frames both an early gathering of followers and their commission to make disciples. Overview sources and context: Matthew 4:12–25 ; Matthew 28:16–20 Verse references: Galilee

capernaum.name: Capernaum
capernaum.text: The opening scene emphasizes Jesus teaching in the synagogue (Mark 1:21). And they went into Capernaum; and straightway on the sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, and taught. Mark 1:21 · King James Version (KJV) Capernaum is a lakeside town that Matthew identifies as Jesus’ residence after he leaves Nazareth. Mark presents its synagogue as a setting for teaching and an encounter with an unclean spirit, followed by healing at Simon and Andrew’s house. The narratives move between worship space, household, and crowded doorway, giving the town a particularly concrete role in the beginnings of Jesus’ ministry. Overview sources and context: Matthew 4:12–17 ; Mark 1:21–34 Verse references: C

sea-of-galilee.name: Sea of Galilee
sea-of-galilee.text: The entry links the fishermen's working place with their call to follow Jesus (Matthew 4; Luke 5). And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers. Matthew 4:18 · King James Version (KJV) The Sea of Galilee is the lake around which fishing, travel, teaching, and several Gospel signs take place. Luke calls it the lake of Gennesaret; John explicitly identifies it also as the sea of Tiberias. Its boats and nets belong to the disciples’ working lives before becoming settings for their encounters with Jesus. These names refer to the same body of water. Overview sources and context: Luke 5:1–1

gethsemane.name: Gethsemane
gethsemane.text: Jesus' prayer before his arrest is this entry's defining scene (Matthew 26:36). Then cometh Jesus with them unto a place called Gethsemane, and saith unto the disciples, Sit ye here, while I go and pray yonder. Matthew 26:36 · King James Version (KJV) Gethsemane is the named place where Matthew situates Jesus’ sorrowful prayer before his arrest. He asks his companions to watch while he prays, but finds them sleeping; Judas then arrives with the arresting party. John separately describes an arrest in a garden across the Kidron brook, without using the name Gethsemane. The passages should be read with their different geographical details intact. Overview sources and context: Matthew 26:30–56 ;

golgotha.name: Golgotha
golgotha.text: This place is identified through Jesus' crucifixion and the cross. And they bring him unto the place Golgotha, which is, being interpreted, The place of a skull. Mark 15:22 · King James Version (KJV) Golgotha is the place of Jesus’ crucifixion, its name explained in the Gospels as the place of a skull. Mark describes the soldiers, divided garments, inscription, and other condemned men; John locates the execution near the city and mentions a nearby garden tomb. These details establish its role in the passion narratives, but do not by themselves identify an exact modern spot. Overview sources and context: Mark 15:20–39 ; John 19:17–42 Verse references: Golgotha

antioch.name: Antioch in Syria
antioch.text: The entry focuses on the church's shared life, support and worship; its commissioning is also an orange theme. And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch. Acts 11:27 · King James Version (KJV) This entry concerns Syrian Antioch, the church center associated with Barnabas and Saul, rather than the Antioch in Pisidia visited later in Acts. Here believers are first called Christians, a collection is sent to help Judean believers, and Barnabas and Saul are commissioned for a journey. Antioch functions as a place of teaching, practical solidarity, and outward mission within the expanding movement. Overview sources and context: Acts 11:19–30 ; Acts 13:1–14 Verse references: Antioc

ephesus.name: Ephesus
ephesus.text: The entry follows disciples and the life of the church addressed in Revelation. And it came to pass, that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul having passed through the upper coasts came to Ephesus: and finding certain disciples, Acts 19:1 · King James Version (KJV) Ephesus is a city where Acts describes Paul’s sustained teaching and a public conflict involving craftsmen who make shrines for Diana, also known as Artemis. The theater becomes the setting of an assembly stirred by religious and economic concerns. Revelation later addresses its church, commending endurance while warning about abandoned love. The city’s biblical portrait therefore includes civic life, mission, and communal self-ex

rome.name: Rome
rome.text: Rome is the destination of Paul's continuing mission and witness (Acts 28). And when we came to Rome, the centurion delivered the prisoners to the captain of the guard: but Paul was suffered to dwell by himself with a soldier that kept him. Acts 28:16 · King James Version (KJV) Rome is the destination of Paul’s journey as a prisoner at the close of Acts. He lives under guard, receives visitors, discusses the Scriptures, and continues teaching about Jesus. The letter to the Romans already addresses believers there and expresses his desire to visit them. Rome thus represents both an existing Christian community and a major destination in the narrative of the gospel’s spread. Overview sources a

things.name: Things
things.text: Noah’s ark · Ark of the covenant · Tabernacle · Temple in Jerusalem · Altar · Lampstand · Incense · Anointing oil · Ephod · Breastpiece · Stone tablets · Manna · Bronze serpent · Passover lamb · Unleavened bread · Scroll · Denarius · Talent (weight and value) · Fig tree · Olive tree · Grapevine · Wheat · Mustard seed · Fishing net · Cross

noahs-ark.name: Noah’s ark
noahs-ark.text: The vessel preserves a household and animals through the flood. Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch. Genesis 6:14 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Noah’s ark is the large wooden vessel in the flood narrative, called a “ship” in this translation. God directs its construction, including compartments and a coating of pitch. It shelters Noah’s household and animals through the flood before they emerge onto dry land. Its narrative role is preservation amid judgment. This vessel is distinct from the much smaller chest called the ark of the covenant. Overview sources and context: Genesis 7:1–16 ; Genesis 8:15–19

ark-of-the-covenant.name: Ark of the covenant
ark-of-the-covenant.text: The sacred chest holds the covenant testimony; its worship setting is distinguished from Noah's vessel. You shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark. Exodus 25:14 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The ark of the covenant is a sacred acacia-wood chest overlaid with gold and carried on poles. Exodus places the covenant testimony inside and describes a golden cover with cherubim above it. It belongs to Israel’s sanctuary worship and later stands in Solomon’s inner sanctuary. Its association with divine presence is central to the narrative; it is a different object from Noah’s flood vessel. Overview sources and context: Exodus 25:10–22 ; 1 Kings 8:6

tabernacle.name: Tabernacle
tabernacle.text: The entry concerns the sanctuary and God's dwelling among worshippers. You shall set up the tabernacle according to the way that it was shown to you on the mountain. Exodus 26:30 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The tabernacle is the constructed sanctuary associated with Israel’s wilderness journeys. Exodus describes curtains, coverings, wooden framing, and furnishings arranged around a holy place and a most holy place. The ark stands behind the separating veil. Its portable form fits the journey narrative, while the cloud and divine glory mark God’s dwelling among the people. “Tabernacle” here names this particular sanctuary rather than any ordinary tent. Overview sources and c

temple.name: Temple in Jerusalem
temple.text: The entry identifies Jerusalem's sanctuary and its worship. So Solomon built the house and finished it. 1 Kings 6:14 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Jerusalem’s temple is the sanctuary called Yahweh’s house in Kings. Solomon’s building contains an inner sanctuary for the ark and uses stone, cedar, and gold. Its history includes destruction by Babylonian forces and a later rebuilding undertaken by the returned community. Ezra records both celebration and grief when the new foundation is laid. References to the first and later temples therefore concern distinct building phases, not one unchanged structure. Overview sources and context: 2 Kings 25:8–17 ; Ezra 3:8–13 Verse referenc

altar.name: Altar
altar.text: Offerings and worship give the altar its function in this entry. Noah built an altar to Yahweh, and took of every clean animal, and of every clean bird, and offered burnt offerings on the altar. Genesis 8:20 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) An altar is a place or constructed structure used for offerings. Genesis presents Noah building one after the flood. Sanctuary instructions describe a bronze-covered altar for burnt offerings and a separate gold-covered altar for incense, with different locations and functions. Materials, size, and permitted offerings depend on the passage. Keeping these distinctions visible prevents the general word “altar” from collapsing several kinds of r

lampstand.name: Lampstand
lampstand.text: The entry describes a sanctuary furnishing maintained for worship. You shall make its lamps seven, and they shall light its lamps to give light to the space in front of it. Exodus 25:37 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The sanctuary lampstand is a hammered-gold furnishing with a central shaft, six branches, and seven lamps. Its floral details include cups shaped like almond blossoms. Priestly care and olive oil keep the sanctuary lamps burning. Revelation later uses seven golden lampstands in a vision and identifies them with seven assemblies. That visionary symbolism should be distinguished from the single seven-lamp furnishing described in Exodus. Overview sources and context:

incense.name: Incense
incense.text: Incense is used in worship and explicitly compared with prayer. You shall make incense of it, a perfume after the art of the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. Exodus 30:35 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Incense is an aromatic preparation burned in worship. Exodus prescribes a sacred blend and regulates its use at the sanctuary, where Aaron burns it in connection with tending the lamps. Its rising smoke also supplies biblical imagery for prayer: Psalm 141 makes the comparison, and Revelation joins incense with the saints’ prayers. The physical compound, its ritual use, and the literary image remain related but distinguishable. Overview sources and context: Psalm 141:

anointing-oil.name: Anointing oil
anointing-oil.text: Consecration and anointing for service are the entry's defining theme. You shall make it into a holy anointing oil, a perfume compounded after the art of the perfumer: it shall be a holy anointing oil. Exodus 30:25 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Anointing oil is oil applied to people or objects in an act of consecration. Exodus gives a particular fragrant preparation for the sanctuary, its equipment, and the priesthood, with restrictions on imitation and ordinary use. Leviticus narrates Moses pouring it on Aaron. Samuel’s anointing of David shows oil in royal commissioning, but that passage does not specify the same formula as the sanctuary instructions. Overview sources and c

ephod.name: Ephod
ephod.text: This entry concerns clothing used in priestly service. He made the ephod of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. Exodus 39:2 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) In the priestly clothing instructions, the ephod is a specially worked garment with shoulder straps and a woven band. Two stones on its shoulders bear the names of Israel’s sons as a memorial before Yahweh. The word also occurs in descriptions of linen ephods, including the one worn by the young Samuel. Those passages should not automatically be pictured as the richly decorated garment prescribed for Aaron. Overview sources and context: Exodus 28:6–14 ; 1 Samuel 2:18 Verse references: Ephod

breastpiece.name: Breastpiece
breastpiece.text: The priest bears Israel's names before God in the sanctuary (Exodus 28:29). Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment on his heart, when he goes in to the holy place, for a memorial before Yahweh continually. Exodus 28:29 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The priestly breastpiece, called a “breastplate of judgment” in this translation, is a square, doubled textile attached to the ephod. Its twelve engraved stones represent Israel’s tribes, whose names Aaron bears over his heart. The instructions also associate it with the Urim and Thummim. It is ceremonial clothing rather than military armor. The narrative explains its representative func

stone-tablets.name: Stone tablets
stone-tablets.text: The tablets bear the covenant and commandments. When he finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, he gave Moses the two tablets of the covenant, stone tablets, written with God’s finger. Exodus 31:18 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The stone tablets are the material witnesses of the covenant given to Moses at Sinai. Exodus describes two tablets written on both sides and attributes their writing to God. Moses breaks the first pair when he sees the golden calf. Deuteronomy recounts replacement tablets bearing the ten commandments and their placement in the ark. Their physical history accompanies the narrative of covenant violation and renewal. Overview sources and context: Exodu

manna.name: Manna
manna.text: The entry describes extraordinary wilderness provision; Jesus' bread-of-life teaching is a distinct green use. The house of Israel called its name “Manna”, and it was like coriander seed, white; and its taste was like wafers with honey. Exodus 16:31 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Manna is the food Israel gathers in the wilderness in Exodus. The narrative gives its appearance and taste, describes daily collection, and makes special provision for Sabbath rest. Deuteronomy treats the experience as instruction in dependence on God. John’s Gospel recalls manna within Jesus’ teaching about the bread of life. These descriptions establish its biblical role without identifying it with

bronze-serpent.name: Bronze serpent
bronze-serpent.text: The opening scene concerns healing and preservation of those bitten (Numbers 21:9); later idolatrous misuse is indigo. Moses made a serpent of bronze, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of bronze, he lived. Numbers 21:9 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The bronze serpent is an object Moses makes at God’s command during an outbreak of deadly snakebites. In Numbers, looking toward the raised serpent brings life to those bitten. Second Kings later reports Hezekiah destroying it because people were burning incense to it. John compares its lifting up with the lifting up of the Son of Man. Its original narrative function and later mi

passover-lamb.name: Passover lamb
passover-lamb.text: The entry centers on Passover deliverance and its stated Christian connection to Christ. Your lamb shall be without defect, a male a year old. You shall take it from the sheep or from the goats. Exodus 12:5 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The Passover animal belongs to the meal and deliverance narrative of Israel’s departure from Egypt. Exodus specifies an unblemished year-old male from sheep or goats, its blood placed on doorposts, and its flesh eaten roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Later instructions connect Passover with the chosen sanctuary. Paul’s description of Christ as “our Passover” is a Christian theological use of this established sacrificial language

unleavened-bread.name: Unleavened bread
unleavened-bread.text: The entry connects the food to a recurring festival of remembrance. They baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought out of Egypt; for it wasn’t leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt, and couldn’t wait, and they had not prepared any food for themselves. Exodus 12:39 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Unleavened bread is bread made without leavening. Exodus connects it with the haste of departure from Egypt and with a recurring festival requiring the removal of yeast. Deuteronomy calls it the bread of affliction and links eating it with remembrance. Paul later uses unleavened bread as an image of sincerity and truth. The festival food and this moral metaphor be

scroll.name: Scroll
scroll.text: The opening scene records the prophetic words given through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 36:4). Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all Yahweh’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book. Jeremiah 36:4 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) A scroll is a roll carrying written text. Jeremiah’s account makes the object especially tangible: Baruch writes with ink, the words are read aloud, the king cuts and burns the roll, and another is written. Luke presents Jesus reading Isaiah in the synagogue, while Revelation depicts a sealed book in a vision. These settings distinguish ordinary textual transmission and public reading from

denarius.name: Denarius
denarius.text: The opening coin occurs in Jesus' kingdom teaching (Matthew 20); the coin itself is not a sacred symbol. When he had agreed with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. Matthew 20:2 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) A denarius is a Roman silver coin appearing in Gospel accounts of wages, prices, debt, and taxation. In Matthew’s vineyard parable, the laborers agree to one denarius for a day’s work. The tax controversy draws attention to a coin’s image and inscription, while the Samaritan pays an innkeeper two denarii. These narrative comparisons help establish scale without turning the coin into a fixed modern currency equivalent. Overview sources and co

talent.name: Talent (weight and value)
talent.text: The opening verse specifies a weight in the sanctuary construction instructions (Exodus 25:39). It shall be made of a talent of pure gold, with all these accessories. Exodus 25:39 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) A talent is a large unit of weight used for precious metal and, in monetary contexts, a substantial sum of value. Exodus uses it in specifying gold for the lampstand. Matthew uses talents in parables about an enormous debt and property entrusted to servants. The latter passage distinguishes the money entrusted from each servant’s ability. Modern meanings of “talent” as a skill should not replace the unit in these scenes. Overview sources and context: Matthew 18:23–35 ;

fig-tree.name: Fig tree
fig-tree.text: The opening proverb teaches wisdom about tending and receiving fruit (Proverbs 27:18). Whoever tends the fig tree shall eat its fruit. He who looks after his master shall be honored. Proverbs 27:18 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The fig tree appears as a cultivated source of fruit and as an image drawn from familiar agricultural life. Proverbs connects tending it with enjoying its produce. Micah pictures people sitting beneath their vines and fig trees in peace. In Mark, Jesus’ encounter with a fruitless fig tree frames events at the temple. Its literary significance therefore depends on the setting rather than a single symbolic meaning in every occurrence. Overview sources an

olive-tree.name: Olive tree
olive-tree.text: The opening olive leaf belongs to the restored living landscape and God's provision (Genesis 8:11). The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters were abated from the earth. Genesis 8:11 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The olive tree belongs to the productive landscape described in Deuteronomy, while olive oil serves practical and ritual purposes elsewhere in Scripture. In Genesis, an olive leaf carried by the dove tells Noah that the floodwaters have receded. Romans uses cultivated and wild olive branches in an extended account of Israel and Gentiles, warning against boasting. The agricultural tree

grapevine.name: Grapevine
grapevine.text: The opening quotation identifies Jesus as the vine and teaches dependence on him (John 15:5). I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. John 15:5 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Grapevines and vineyards provide fruit and wine and recur throughout biblical agricultural language. The spies bring a cluster from Canaan as evidence of the land’s produce. Isaiah’s vineyard song develops cultivation into a critique of Israel and Judah’s failure to produce justice. John’s Gospel uses vine and branches to describe the disciples’ dependence on Jesus. These distinct applications grow from the concrete rel

wheat.name: Wheat
wheat.text: The opening grain image belongs to Jesus' teaching about his death and fruitfulness (John 12:24). Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. John 12:24 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Wheat is a cultivated grain connected with food, harvest, and household provision. Ruth’s gleaning continues through both barley and wheat harvests, grounding the story in agricultural work. Jesus’ parable of wheat and weeds uses a field and its eventual harvest to address judgment. In John, the grain that falls and bears fruit accompanies teaching about Jesus’ coming death and the cost of follo

mustard-seed.name: Mustard seed
mustard-seed.text: The cited seed comparisons teach about the kingdom and faith. It is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took and put in his own garden. It grew and became a large tree, and the birds of the sky live in its branches.” Luke 13:19 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The mustard seed is a small seed used in Jesus’ comparisons. The kingdom parables emphasize the striking movement from a small beginning to a plant offering shelter to birds. Another saying compares faith to a mustard seed. The passages use recognizable gardening imagery to teach; they do not name a modern botanical species. Their point can be described without assigning an unsupported scientific identification to the

fishing-net.name: Fishing net
fishing-net.text: Leaving the nets marks the disciples' answer to Jesus' call (Mark 1:18). Immediately they left their nets, and followed him. Mark 1:18 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) Fishing nets are working equipment in the lives of several disciples. Gospel scenes show them being cast, washed, mended, and strained by a heavy catch. Leaving the nets marks a response to Jesus’ call. Matthew also compares the kingdom to a dragnet whose mixed catch is sorted on shore, explaining it in terms of judgment. The occupational setting and the parable’s imagery give the same ordinary tool different narrative functions. Overview sources and context: Luke 5:1–11 ; Matthew 13:47–50 Verse references: Fishin

cross.name: Cross
cross.text: Jesus' death, salvation and discipleship define the cross in this entry. Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” John 19:19 · World English Bible Classic (public domain) The cross is the instrument of execution on which Jesus is crucified in the Gospel narratives. John describes the inscription, the people standing nearby, and Jesus’ death. Jesus also uses carrying a cross in teaching about discipleship, while Paul speaks of the message of the cross as God’s saving power. These uses connect a physical instrument of death with the meaning Christian texts give to Jesus’ death and following him. Overview sources and conte

god-and-creation.text: Read this category on its own → God and the Most High · The Son and the Lord Jesus Christ · The Holy Spirit and the Spirit of truth

god.name: God and the Most High
god.text: The entry identifies God as Creator and the Most High; shared divine titles retain their contextual distinctions. Divine God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. John 4:24 · World English Bible God is the one worshipped, the Creator to whom heavenly beings give glory. “Most High” and “Almighty” are divine titles in the cited passages, not names for additional members of a spiritual hierarchy. Read in context: Revelation 4:8–11 ; Daniel 4:34–35 Verse references: God and the Most High

son.name: The Son and the Lord Jesus Christ
son.text: The entry identifies the Son and Lord Jesus Christ, distinguished from created angels. Divine When he again brings in the firstborn into the world he says, “Let all the angels of God worship him.” Hebrews 1:6 · World English Bible Hebrews distinguishes the Son from the angels who worship and serve. Colossians places the creation of visible and invisible things, including thrones and powers, through him and for him. Read in context: Hebrews 1:1–14 ; Colossians 1:15–17 Verse references: The Son and the Lord Jesus Christ

holy-spirit.name: Holy Spirit
holy-spirit.text: This entry studies a designation associated with the Holy Spirit; its stated contextual and interpretive qualifications remain in force. title or designation But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you. John 14:26 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Holy Spirit is the familiar New Testament designation for the Spirit associated here with the Father’s sending, Jesus’ name, teaching, and remembrance. “Holy Ghost” is an older English translation of the same expression, not another spirit. Matthew places the Holy Spirit alongside Father and Son in the baptismal commission. The entries in this s
