angels-and-heavenly-beings.text: Read this category on its own → Angels and ministering spirits · Michael and the title archangel · Gabriel · The angel of the LORD · Cherubim · Seraphim · The four living creatures · Watchers and holy ones · Angels who guard · The heavenly host · The seven angels before God · The destroyer

angels.name: ✦ Angels and ministering spirits
angels.text: The entry focuses on heavenly help and ministry to those inheriting salvation (Hebrews 1:14). Heavenly servants Aren’t they all serving spirits, sent out to do service for the sake of those who will inherit salvation? Hebrews 1:14 · World English Bible Angels serve God and are sent for the benefit of people. Their work includes announcing good news, helping, and carrying out commands; the angel in Revelation directs worship to God. Read in context: Luke 2:9–15 ; Revelation 22:8–9 Verse references: Angels and ministering spirits

michael.name: ✦ Michael and the title archangel
michael.text: Michael's entry centers on conflict with the adversary (Jude 9; Revelation 12); this color describes the battle, not an evil identity. Named heavenly being But Michael, the archangel, when contending with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, dared not bring against him an abusive condemnation, but said, “May the Lord rebuke you!” Jude 1:9 · World English Bible Michael is explicitly called an archangel. Daniel calls him one of the chief princes and a protector of Daniel’s people; Revelation depicts him leading his angels against the dragon. Read in context: Daniel 10:13, 21 ; Daniel 12:1 ; Revelation 12:7–9 Verse references: Michael and the title archangel

gabriel.name: ✦ Gabriel
gabriel.text: Gabriel brings announcements and explains visions (Daniel 8–9; Luke 1). Named angel The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God. I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.” Luke 1:19 · World English Bible Gabriel brings and explains messages from God. He interprets Daniel’s vision and announces the births of John and Jesus; these passages call him an angel but do not give him the title archangel. Read in context: Daniel 8:15–17 ; Daniel 9:21–23 ; Luke 1:26–33 Verse references: Gabriel

angel-of-the-lord.name: ✦ The angel of the LORD
angel-of-the-lord.text: The burning-bush appearance introduces God's call to Moses; the messenger's identity remains qualified. Messenger title with contextual ambiguity The LORD’s angel appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the middle of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed. Exodus 3:2 · World English Bible At the burning bush, the narrative moves from the angel’s appearance to God speaking. In Judges, the messenger directs an offering to the LORD; the title does not by itself settle whether every occurrence refers to the same being or how the messenger relates to God. Read in context: Exodus 3:4–6 ; Judges 13:16–22 ; Luke 2:9–11 Verse references: The angel of

cherubim.name: ✦ Cherubim
cherubim.text: The opening scene guards the way to life after expulsion (Genesis 3:24); the color marks judgment, not demonic identity. Heavenly beings and sanctuary representations So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life. Genesis 3:24 · World English Bible Cherubim guard the way to the tree of life and appear with God’s glory in Ezekiel. The cherubim made for the ark are crafted representations; Ezekiel explicitly identifies the living creatures he saw as cherubim. Read in context: Exodus 25:18–22 ; Ezekiel 10:18–22 Verse references: Cherubim

seraphim.name: ✦ Seraphim
seraphim.text: The entry emphasizes the seraphim proclaiming God's holiness in worship (Isaiah 6). Heavenly beings in a vision Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings. With two he covered his face. With two he covered his feet. With two he flew. Isaiah 6:2 · World English Bible The seraphim proclaim the LORD’s holiness in Isaiah’s throne vision. One brings a coal to Isaiah’s lips and announces cleansing before Isaiah receives his commission. Read in context: Isaiah 6:3–8 Verse references: Seraphim

living-creatures.name: ✦ The four living creatures
living-creatures.text: The four creatures worship around God's throne (Revelation 4). Heavenly beings in visions The first creature was like a lion, the second creature like a calf, the third creature had a face like a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle. Revelation 4:7 · World English Bible Revelation places these worshipping creatures around the throne. Ezekiel identifies his living creatures as cherubim, while Revelation describes its own vision; their shared imagery should not be turned into a detailed hierarchy that neither passage supplies. Read in context: Revelation 4:6–9 ; Ezekiel 10:20–22 Verse references: The four living creatures

watchers.name: ✦ Watchers and holy ones
watchers.text: The watcher announces God's decree within a dream (Daniel 4). Heavenly titles in Daniel’s vision “‘The sentence is by the decree of the watchers and the demand by the word of the holy ones, to the intent that the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he will, and sets up over it the lowest of men.’ Daniel 4:17 · World English Bible A holy watcher descends in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream to announce judgment on his pride. Daniel identifies the sentence as the Most High’s decree; this chapter gives neither personal names nor a story of rebellious Watchers. Read in context: Daniel 4:13–17, 23–25 Verse references: Watchers and holy ones

guarding-angels.name: ✦ Angels who guard
guarding-angels.text: The quoted promise concerns God-given protection (Psalm 91:11). Angelic function For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways. Psalm 91:11 · World English Bible The psalm describes angels carrying out God’s protection. Jesus also speaks of the little ones’ angels before the Father; these texts do not name each person’s angel or provide a separate ranked order called Guardian Angels. Read in context: Psalm 91:12 ; Matthew 18:10 Verse references: Angels who guard

heavenly-host.name: ✦ The heavenly host
heavenly-host.text: The heavenly multitude praises God at Jesus' birth (Luke 2:13–14). Collective title Suddenly, there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army praising God and saying, Luke 2:13 · World English Bible At Jesus’ birth, the heavenly host joins the messenger in praising God. The collective title describes an assembled multitude, without supplying individual names or a complete organization of heaven. Read in context: Luke 2:14–15 ; 1 Kings 22:19 Verse references: The heavenly host

seven-angels.name: ✦ The seven angels before God
seven-angels.text: The seven angels receive trumpets in a judgment vision (Revelation 8); no personal names are inferred. Angelic group I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them. Revelation 8:2 · World English Bible These angels receive trumpets in Revelation’s unfolding judgments. The verse does not list their names, and it should not be completed with names supplied by a different book or later tradition. Read in context: Revelation 8:6 Verse references: The seven angels before God

destroyer.name: The destroyer
destroyer.text: The entry describes an agent of Passover judgment; it does not identify that agent with Satan or Abaddon. Agent of judgment For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians; and when he sees the blood on the lintel, and on the two door posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to come in to your houses to strike you. Exodus 12:23 · World English Bible The Passover account describes the LORD preventing the destroyer from entering the blood-marked houses. Hebrews recalls the same deliverance; neither passage supplies a personal name or identifies the destroyer with Abaddon. Read in context: Exodus 12:21–29 ; Hebrews 11:28 Related: Abaddon and Apollyon Vers

evil-spirits-and-adversaries.name: Evil spirits and adversaries
evil-spirits-and-adversaries.text: Read this category on its own → Satan, the devil, the tempter and the accuser · Demons and unclean spirits · Beelzebul · Legion · Belial · Angels who sinned · A lying spirit · The evil spirit troubling Saul · A spirit of divination · The spirit of antichrist and the spirit of error

satan.name: ✕ Satan, the devil, the tempter and the accuser
satan.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Named adversary and associated titles Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. Matthew 4:1 · World English Bible The temptation narrative calls the opponent the devil, the tempter, and Satan. Job depicts Satan challenging Job’s faithfulness, while Revelation identifies the dragon as the devil and Satan and describes his accusing work. Wisdom of Solomon is deuterocanonical and is included in the Saints.Bible collection. Read in context: Matthew 4:3, 10–11 ; Job 1:6–12 ; Revelation 12:9–10 ; Wisdom of Sol

demons.name: ✕ Demons and unclean spirits
demons.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Spiritual opponents At once Jesus gave them permission. The unclean spirits came out and entered into the pigs. The herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea, and they were drowned in the sea. Mark 5:13 · World English Bible Mark calls the same group demons and unclean spirits as Jesus frees the afflicted man. Revelation also calls its frog-like unclean spirits spirits of demons; these passages describe their actions without giving an origin story for every demon. Read in context: Mark 5:2–15 ; Revelation 16:13–14 Verse

beelzebul.name: ✕ Beelzebul
beelzebul.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Title or name for the ruler of demons But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.” Matthew 12:24 · World English Bible The name occurs in the opponents’ accusation about Jesus’ exorcisms. Jesus answers by discussing Satan’s divided kingdom and attributes his own work to God’s Spirit; the passage gives no independent biography of Beelzebul. Read in context: Matthew 12:25–28 Related: Baal Zebub Verse references: Beelzebul

legion.name: ✕ Legion
legion.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Collective self-designation He asked him, “What is your name?” He said to him, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” Mark 5:9 · World English Bible The answer explains itself in terms of many spirits. In this narrative, Legion is a collective designation; the text does not introduce a separate named commander over all demons. Read in context: Mark 5:8–13 Verse references: Legion

belial.name: ✕ Belial
belial.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Adversarial name or designation What agreement does Christ have with Belial? Or what portion does a believer have with an unbeliever? 2 Corinthians 6:15 · World English Bible Paul places Belial opposite Christ within a series of contrasts between righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, and God’s temple and idols. The verse supplies no rank, appearance, or history for the designation. Read in context: 2 Corinthians 6:14–16 Verse references: Belial

angels-who-sinned.name: ✕ Angels who sinned
angels-who-sinned.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Angels under judgment Angels who didn’t keep their first domain, but deserted their own dwelling place, he has kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day. Jude 1:6 · World English Bible Jude and 2 Peter describe angels held for judgment after wrongdoing. Neither cited passage gives their individual names; combining them with every other account of demons or giants would go beyond what those verses explicitly say. Read in context: 2 Peter 2:4–5 Verse references: Angels who sinned

lying-spirit.name: ✕ A lying spirit
lying-spirit.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Narrative role A spirit came out and stood before Yahweh, and said, ‘I will entice him.’ 1 Kings 22:21 · World English Bible Classic In Micaiah’s vision, the spirit proposes to deceive Ahab through his prophets and is permitted to do so. “Lying spirit” describes its function in this judgment narrative; no personal name is given. Read in context: 1 Kings 22:19–23 Verse references: A lying spirit

evil-spirit-saul.name: ✕ The evil spirit troubling Saul
evil-spirit-saul.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Narrative description Now the LORD’s Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the LORD troubled him. 1 Samuel 16:14 · World English Bible The narrative sets Saul’s distress beside the LORD’s Spirit coming upon David. David’s music brings relief and the spirit departs; the text leaves the spirit unnamed and does not give a general diagnostic rule for human illness. Read in context: 1 Samuel 16:13, 23 Verse references: The evil spirit troubling Saul

spirit-of-divination.name: ✕ A spirit of divination
spirit-of-divination.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Narrative description As we were going to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling. Acts 16:16 · World English Bible The spirit’s activity is tied to the enslaved girl’s profitable fortune-telling. Paul commands it to leave in Jesus Christ’s name, and its departure ends her owners’ source of income. Read in context: Acts 16:17–19 Verse references: A spirit of divination

spirit-of-antichrist.name: The spirit of antichrist and the spirit of error
spirit-of-antichrist.text: The entry concerns spiritual opposition, deception, temptation or wrongdoing in its cited passages; the existing limits on identity remain in force. Descriptions of opposition and false teaching and every spirit who doesn’t confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not of God; and this is the spirit of the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that it comes. Now it is in the world already. 1 John 4:3 · World English Bible John tests spiritual claims by their confession concerning Jesus and connects error with false prophets. The same letter speaks of many antichrists, so these expressions should not be converted into a list of individually named demons. Read in context: 1 John 4:1–6 ;

powers-and-authorities.name: Powers and authorities
powers-and-authorities.text: Read this category on its own → Principalities · Powers · World rulers of darkness · Thrones · Dominions · Authorities · The princes of Persia and Greece · The prince of the power of the air · Elemental spirits or rudiments of the world These entries follow biblical terms and their contexts. Translation labels can overlap; the passages do not establish a complete hierarchy or mutually exclusive spiritual classes.

principalities.name: Principalities
principalities.text: The opening passage reveals God's wisdom through the assembly (Ephesians 3:10); hostile uses elsewhere must be distinguished. to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places, Ephesians 3:10 · World English Bible Classic Principalities appear as recipients of the revelation of God’s wisdom through the assembly. In spiritual-conflict passages, they appear among opponents and among the powers subjected to triumph. Context determines their portrayal: these passages do not establish that every principality is evil, assign individual territories, or explain a fixed rank. The underlying Greek word

powers.name: Powers
powers.text: The opening passage emphasizes the exalted Christ and the powers' subjection to him (1 Peter 3:22). who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him. 1 Peter 3:22 · World English Bible Classic Powers are subject to the ascended Christ. Romans 8:38–39 includes powers among everything unable to separate believers from God’s love in Christ. These verses give no appearance, distinctive office, or fixed rank and do not label every power hostile. In 1 Peter 3:22, “authorities” and “powers” represent different Greek words. Elsewhere, including Ephesians 6:12, WEB Classic uses “powers” for the word family rendered “authorities” her

world-rulers-darkness.name: World rulers of darkness
world-rulers-darkness.text: The cited passage explicitly concerns spiritual opposition (Ephesians 6:12). For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world’s rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Ephesians 6:12 · World English Bible Classic These rulers belong to the spiritual opposition against which believers are instructed to stand using God’s armor: truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, God’s word, and prayer. The passage distinguishes this struggle from flesh and blood. It supplies no individual names, number, territorial map, or hierarchy and does not identify particular huma

thrones.name: Thrones
thrones.text: The opening passage includes thrones within what was created (Colossians 1:16); it gives no fixed angelic rank. For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. Colossians 1:16 · World English Bible Classic Thrones appear in a passage emphasizing Christ’s relationship to all creation, including its invisible dimensions. They belong within what was created through him and for him. The passage provides no appearance, personal names, distinctive duties, or rank relative to the other terms. It does not identify thrones with Ezekie

dominions.name: Dominions
dominions.text: The opening passage includes dominions within creation (Colossians 1:16); other uses require context. For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, visible things and invisible things, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. Colossians 1:16 · World English Bible Classic Dominions express the extent of Christ’s creative sovereignty. Ephesians 1:20–21 also places the risen Christ far above all dominion. Neither passage explains a dominion’s particular assignment, appearance, or position within a hierarchy, and neither labels all dominions hostile. Read in context: Ephesians 1:20–21 ; Colossians 1:15–2

authorities.name: Authorities
authorities.text: The cited opening emphasizes the authorities' subjection to the exalted Christ (1 Peter 3:22). who is at the right hand of God, having gone into heaven, angels and authorities and powers being made subject to him. 1 Peter 3:22 · World English Bible Classic Authorities appear alongside angels and powers in a declaration of Christ’s exaltation and supremacy. The point is their subjection to him, rather than a description of their individual activities. The passages give no fixed hierarchy or distinctive appearance. This entry concerns heavenly contexts; the same English word also describes earthly authority elsewhere. The Greek word family rendered “authorities” here is rendered “powers” in WE

princes-persia-greece.name: The princes of Persia and Greece
princes-persia-greece.text: The entry describes conflict involving the princes in Daniel 10 without inventing personal names. Unnamed opponents in a heavenly conflict Then he said, “Do you know why I have come to you? Now I will return to fight with the prince of Persia. When I go out, behold, the prince of Greece will come.” Daniel 10:20 · World English Bible Daniel’s messenger describes conflict involving these princes and Michael. Their setting points to a heavenly dimension of earthly kingdoms, but the chapter gives no personal names and does not call them members of a fully defined territorial hierarchy. Read in context: Daniel 10:13, 21 Verse references: The princes of Persia and Greece

prince-air-world.name: The prince of the power of the air
prince-air-world.text: The title appears in an account of spiritual opposition and disobedience (Ephesians 2:2). Adversarial title in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience. Ephesians 2:2 · World English Bible Paul describes a spiritual power at work in disobedience before contrasting it with God’s mercy. Jesus also speaks of the prince of the world; these are functional titles, not additional personal names supplied by the verses. Read in context: Ephesians 2:1–5 ; John 14:30 Verse references: The prince of the power of the air

elemental-spirits.name: Elemental spirits or rudiments of the world
elemental-spirits.text: The passage warns against deceptive teaching; the spirits/rudiments translation question stays open (Colossians 2:8). Translation-sensitive expression Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elemental spirits of the world, and not after Christ. Colossians 2:8 · World English Bible Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. Colossians 2:8 · King James Version The translation difference matters: one edition renders the expression as elemental spirits, another as rudiments. The context concerns captivity to

gods-and-sons-of-god.name: Gods and sons of God
gods-and-sons-of-god.text: Read this category on its own → Gods, idols and divine claims · The gods in Psalm 82 · God language applied to a human representative · Sons of God · Baal · Asherah · Baal and Asherah: does Scripture describe a marriage? · Queen of Heaven · Ashtoreth · Chemosh · Milcom · Molech · Dagon · Bel and Nebo · Baal Zebub · Zeus, Hermes and Artemis

gods.name: Gods, idols and divine claims
gods.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Context-dependent terminology Therefore concerning the eating of things sacrificed to idols, we know that no idol is anything in the world, and that there is no other God but one. 1 Corinthians 8:4 · World English Bible Scripture records things and persons called gods while distinguishing them from the one God. Paul also connects idolatrous sacrifice with demons; this does not supply a separate demon-name equivalence for every deity mentioned in the Bible. Read in context: 1 Corinthians 8:5–6 ; 1 Corinthians 10:19–21 ; Deuteronomy 32:16–17 Verse refere

gods-psalm82.name: The gods in Psalm 82
gods-psalm82.text: Psalm 82 condemns unjust judgment; the identity of those addressed remains an interpretive question. Divine-council or judicial language I said, “You are gods, all of you are sons of the Most High.” Psalm 82:6 · World English Bible The psalm condemns unjust judgment and announces death for those it addresses. Whether its gods are read as heavenly beings or human judges requires interpretation; Jesus quotes the passage without giving a list of spirit names. Read in context: Psalm 82:1–8 ; John 10:34–36 Verse references: The gods in Psalm 82

god-language-humans.name: God language applied to a human representative
god-language-humans.text: Moses is commissioned to represent God before Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1); the language does not make him a new deity. Human role The LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I have made you as God to Pharaoh; and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.” Exodus 7:1 · World English Bible Moses represents God before Pharaoh and Aaron speaks as his prophet. This use of divine language describes a commissioned human role rather than introducing another heavenly being. Read in context: Exodus 7:2, 6–7 Verse references: God language applied to a human representative

sons-of-god.name: Sons of God
sons-of-god.text: The opening Job passage describes joyful praise at creation (Job 38:7); other uses of the expression remain distinct. Context-dependent collective expression when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy? Job 38:7 · World English Bible Job places the sons of God at creation’s celebration and before the LORD. Genesis 6 uses the expression without explaining their identity, while Romans applies children of God language to believers; these contexts should not be flattened into one class. Read in context: Job 1:6 ; Genesis 6:1–4 ; Romans 8:14–17 Related: Overview: giant peoples and overlapping names · Nephilim Baal, Asherah, and their relationship in Scripture Ver

baal.name: Baal
baal.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. They took the bull which was given them, and they dressed it, and called on the name of Baal from morning even until noon, saying, ‘Baal, hear us!’ But there was no voice, and nobody answered. They leaped about the altar which was made. 1 Kings 18:26 · World English Bible Classic In the Mount Carmel account, Baal is worshipped as a god whose prophets call upon him to answer. Elijah challenges Israel to choose whom to follow. Baal’s worshippers receive no answer, while Yahweh answers Elijah with fire, and the people acknowledge Yahweh as God. Read in co

asherah.name: Asherah
asherah.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. He brought out the Asherah from Yahweh’s house, outside of Jerusalem, to the brook Kidron, and burned it at the brook Kidron, and beat it to dust, and cast its dust on the graves of the common people. 2 Kings 23:6 · World English Bible Classic Here, “the Asherah” is a physical worship object removed and destroyed during Josiah’s reforms. Judges 6:25–26 likewise describes an Asherah beside Baal’s altar that Gideon must cut down and use as wood. These passages present its removal as part of turning from prohibited worship to Yahweh. Read in context: 2 Ki

baal-asherah-marriage.name: Baal and Asherah: does Scripture describe a marriage?
baal-asherah-marriage.text: The cited accounts concern rival worship; the heading's marriage question does not establish a biblical marriage narrative. Now therefore send, and gather to me all Israel to Mount Carmel, and four hundred fifty of the prophets of Baal, and four hundred of the prophets of the Asherah, who eat at Jezebel’s table. 1 Kings 18:19 · World English Bible Classic Scripture names Baal and Asherah together in accounts of worship. Their prophets appear together here; Judges 6:25 places an Asherah beside Baal’s altar, and 2 Kings 23:4 mentions vessels made for both. These passages establish an association in worship. The Bible does not explicitly identify Baal and Asherah as husband and wife or narrate

queen-of-heaven.name: Queen of Heaven
queen-of-heaven.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Old Testament worship title The children gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead their dough, to make cakes to the queen of heaven, and to pour out drink offerings unto other gods, that they may provoke me to anger. Jeremiah 7:18 · King James Version Jeremiah describes the Queen of Heaven as a recipient of worship involving cakes, incense, drink offerings, and vows. Children, fathers, and women participate in the preparations. In chapter 44, Judeans living in Egypt defend this worship by associating it with their former prospe

ashtoreth.name: Ashtoreth
ashtoreth.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. 1 Kings 11:5 · World English Bible Classic Ashtoreth is named as the goddess of the Sidonians. Solomon’s pursuit of her forms part of his turning away from Yahweh. Josiah later defiled the high place Solomon had built for her. Read in context: 1 Kings 11:5, 33 ; 2 Kings 23:13 Verse references: Ashtoreth

chemosh.name: Chemosh
chemosh.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. Jeremiah 48:13 · World English Bible Classic Chemosh is named as the god of Moab. Solomon built a high place for him near Jerusalem, and Josiah later defiled it. Jeremiah foretells Moab’s shame over Chemosh and his captivity with his priests and princes. Read in context: 1 Kings 11:7, 33 ; 2 Kings 23:13 ; Jeremiah 48:7, 13 Verse references: Chemosh

milcom.name: Milcom
milcom.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. because they have forsaken me, and have worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon. They have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in my eyes, and to keep my statutes and my ordinances, as David his father did. 1 Kings 11:33 · World English Bible Classic Milcom is named as the god of the Ammonites. Solomon followed him, and his worship is among the acts of unfaithfulness named in the announcement that Solomon’s kingdom would be divided. Josiah later defiled the high

molech.name: Molech
molech.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. You shall not give any of your children as a sacrifice to Molech. You shall not profane the name of your God. I am Yahweh. Leviticus 18:21 · World English Bible Classic Molech is associated with the forbidden offering of children. Leviticus condemns this practice, and Jeremiah describes sons and daughters being passed through fire to Molech in the Valley of Hinnom. Josiah defiled Topheth to prevent it. Read in context: Leviticus 20:2–5 ; Jeremiah 32:35 ; 2 Kings 23:10 Verse references: Molech

dagon.name: Dagon
dagon.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Named deity represented by an image The Philistines took God’s ark, and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it by Dagon. 1 Samuel 5:2 · World English Bible Classic Dagon’s image falls before the ark and is found broken. The story displays the LORD’s supremacy in a rival sanctuary; the material image should be distinguished from an explicit appearance of a spirit. Read in context: 1 Samuel 5:3–7 Verse references: Dagon

bel-nebo.name: Bel and Nebo
bel-nebo.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Named deities and carried idols Bel bows down. Nebo stoops. Their idols are carried by animals, and on the livestock. The things that you carried around are heavy loads, a burden for the weary. Isaiah 46:1 · World English Bible The idols must be carried and cannot rescue their worshippers. The contrast is with God, who carries and delivers his people; these verses do not turn Bel and Nebo into named ranks of demons. Read in context: Isaiah 46:2–9 Verse references: Bel and Nebo

baal-zebub.name: Baal Zebub
baal-zebub.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Named deity of Ekron Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover from this sickness.” 2 Kings 1:2 · World English Bible Ahaziah’s appeal to Ekron’s god prompts a rebuke for failing to seek Israel’s God. The similar Gospel name Beelzebul belongs in its own narrative setting rather than being silently merged with this account. Read in context: 2 Kings 1:3–4, 16 Related: Beelzebul Verse references: Ba

zeus-hermes-artemis.name: Zeus, Hermes and Artemis
zeus-hermes-artemis.text: The entry concerns false worship, prohibited practices or their judgment. This does not identify a deity or idol as a separately named demon. Named deities in accounts of human worship They called Barnabas “Zeus” and Paul “Hermes,” because he was the chief speaker. Acts 14:12 · New American Bible Revised Edition When they heard this they were filled with anger, and cried out, saying, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Acts 19:28 · World English Bible The people of Lystra mistake Paul and Barnabas for gods, an identification the apostles reject. Ephesus defends Artemis’s worship and shrine trade; the accounts report human religious claims rather than personal encounters with these deities.

giants-and-the-dead.name: Giants and the dead
giants-and-the-dead.text: Read this category on its own → Overview: giant peoples and overlapping names · Nephilim · Anakim and the descendants of Anak · Rephaim · Emim · Zamzummim / Zamzummites · Og king of Bashan · Goliath · Shades and the departed dead · The giants of old in Sirach

giant-peoples-overview.name: Overview: giant peoples and overlapping names
giant-peoples-overview.text: This overview identifies human peoples and their overlapping names, without assigning demonic identities. These also are considered to be Rephaim, as the Anakim; but the Moabites call them Emim. Deuteronomy 2:11 · World English Bible Classic These five names describe biblical peoples or groups, not five defined biological species. Deuteronomy counts the Emim and Anakim among the Rephaim and identifies Zamzummim as the Ammonite name for earlier Rephaim inhabitants. Nephilim appear in Genesis 6:4 and in the spies’ report in Numbers 13:33; the latter’s link to Anak’s descendants belongs to the report the narrative calls evil. The accounts concern formidable peoples, God’s authority over nations

nephilim.name: Nephilim
nephilim.text: The entry concerns ancient figures in a human genealogy and narrative; disputed origins do not establish a demon class. Ancient figures with debated origins The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bore children to them; the same were the mighty men that were of old, the men of renown. Genesis 6:4 · JPS 1917 There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown. Genesis 6:4 · King James Version The Masoretic Hebrew term is preserved as Nephilim

anakim.name: Anakim and the descendants of Anak
anakim.text: The entry explicitly concerns a people and human lineage. Human lineage and tall people And they went up into the South, and came unto Hebron; and Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were there.--Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.-- Numbers 13:22 · JPS 1917 Anak’s descendants are named among the people encountered in Canaan. Their stature contributes to Israel’s fear, but these passages present a people and lineage rather than a class of disembodied spirits. Read in context: Numbers 13:28, 32–33 ; Deuteronomy 2:10–11 Verse references: Anakim and the descendants of Anak

rephaim.name: Rephaim
rephaim.text: The territorial entry concerns peoples, rulers and land; poetic departed-dead usage is treated separately. (For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron. Isn’t it in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its width, after the cubit of a man.) Deuteronomy 3:11 · World English Bible Classic The Rephaim appear among peoples defeated in Genesis 14:5 and among those listed in God’s land promise to Abram. Deuteronomy connects the name with the Emim, Anakim, Zamzummim, and Og of Bashan. Og’s bedstead dimensions are not a stated measurement of his height. These territorial accounts should be disti

emim.name: Emim
emim.text: The context includes God's instruction not to seize Moab's land (Deuteronomy 2:9–11). These also are considered to be Rephaim, as the Anakim; but the Moabites call them Emim. Deuteronomy 2:11 · World English Bible Classic The preceding verse describes the Emim as a great and numerous people, as tall as the Anakim, who formerly inhabited the region discussed in the account of Moab. Genesis 14:5 names them at Shaveh Kiriathaim. Emim and Rephaim overlap here: Emim is the Moabite name for these people. Their mention accompanies God’s instruction that Israel must not seize Moab’s land, which he had given to Lot’s descendants. Read in context: Deuteronomy 2:9–11 ; Genesis 14:5 Verse references: Em

zamzummim.name: Zamzummim / Zamzummites
zamzummim.text: The context includes God's instruction not to seize Ammon's land (Deuteronomy 2:19–21). That also is accounted a land of Rephaim: Rephaim dwelt therein aforetime; but the Ammonites call them Zamzummim, a people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakim; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead; Deuteronomy 2:20–21 · JPS 1917 Zamzummim is the Ammonite name for the Rephaim who previously inhabited their land. The passage describes them as numerous and tall like the Anakim and recounts their replacement by the Ammonites. Israel is told not to attack Ammon or take its land, which God had given to Lot’s descendants. Zamzummites is an alternative En

og.name: Og king of Bashan
og.text: The entry recounts Israel's victory and deliverance from a human king (Deuteronomy 3); it does not call him a demon. Human king associated with the Rephaim (For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron. Isn’t it in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its width, after the cubit of a man.) Deuteronomy 3:11 · World English Bible Og is a king defeated in Israel’s advance, with his bedstead used to emphasize his exceptional scale. The account identifies him with the Rephaim and treats him as a ruler with a people and territory. Read in context: Deuteronomy 3:1–13 Verse references: Og king of

goliath.name: Goliath
goliath.text: The overview emphasizes deliverance by the Lord rather than superior weapons (1 Samuel 17:45–50). Human warrior A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span went out. 1 Samuel 17:4 · World English Bible Goliath is the armed Philistine champion confronted by David. His defeat points to deliverance by the LORD rather than superior weaponry; the story does not identify him as a demon. Read in context: 1 Samuel 17:45–50 Verse references: Goliath

shades.name: Shades and the departed dead
shades.text: The poem portrays fallen rulers in a judgment taunt (Isaiah 14); it does not turn the human dead into demons. Human dead in poetic imagery The nether-world from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming; the shades are stirred up for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; all the kings of the nations are raised up from their thrones. Isaiah 14:9 · JPS 1917 The Hebrew here uses rephaim for the shades who greet the fallen king in the realm of the dead. The poem identifies them with former rulers; sharing this word with the territorial Rephaim passages does not prove that giant peoples became demons. Read in context: Isaiah 14:4, 9–11 Related: Rephaim, Emim and Zamzummim Verse r

ancient-giants.name: The giants of old in Sirach
ancient-giants.text: Sirach 16:7 recalls rebellion that did not escape judgment. Ancient rebels remembered in wisdom teaching He was not pacified toward the giants of old time, who revolted in their strength. Sirach 16:7 · World English Bible Classic Sirach recalls ancient giants as an example of strength that did not escape divine judgment. This verse does not provide their personal names or identify them as the origin of demons. Sirach is deuterocanonical and is included in the Saints.Bible collection. Verse references: The giants of old in Sirach

dragons-and-visionary-images.name: Dragons and visionary images
dragons-and-visionary-images.text: Read this category on its own → The dragon and the ancient serpent in Revelation · The serpent in Eden · The dragon of Bel and the Dragon · Leviathan · Rahab in the sea imagery · Pharaoh as the great monster · Behemoth · Daniel’s four beasts · The beasts in Revelation · Abaddon and Apollyon · Death and Hades · The seven Spirits of God · Wormwood

dragon.name: ✕ The dragon and the ancient serpent in Revelation
dragon.text: Revelation explicitly identifies this adversarial dragon as Satan (Revelation 12:9). Symbol explicitly identified with Satan The great dragon was thrown down, the old serpent, he who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was thrown down to the earth, and his angels were thrown down with him. Revelation 12:9 · World English Bible Revelation explicitly identifies this dragon as the devil and Satan. He deceives and opposes God’s people, and the later vision shows his defeat; this identification should not automatically be applied to every biblical monster or serpent. Read in context: Revelation 12:10–17 ; Revelation 20:1–3, 10 Related: Satan, the devil, the tempter

eden-serpent.name: The serpent in Eden
eden-serpent.text: The entry concerns deception, temptation and judgment in Genesis 3; Genesis does not itself name the serpent Satan. Creature in the temptation narrative Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” Genesis 3:1 · World English Bible The serpent challenges God’s command and deceives the woman before receiving judgment. Genesis 3 does not itself use the name Satan; Revelation explicitly identifies its own old-serpent figure with Satan. Read in context: Genesis 3:4–15 ; Revelation 12:9 Related: The dragon and the ancient serpent in Revelation Verse references:

bel-and-the-dragon.name: The dragon of Bel and the Dragon
bel-and-the-dragon.text: The story exposes idolatry; this dragon is not identified with Revelation's Satan. Deuterocanonical addition to Daniel; Catholic and Orthodox canons In that same place there was a great dragon which the people of Babylon worshiped. Daniel (Greek) 14:23 / Bel and the Dragon 23 · World English Bible Classic After Daniel exposes the deception surrounding Bel’s idol, the king points to a living dragon worshiped by the Babylonians. Daniel refuses to worship it and kills it with a mixture of pitch, fat, and hair. The narrative contrasts a creature treated as a god with the living God whom Daniel worships. The dragon is distinct from Bel’s manufactured idol and is not identified here as Satan or a

leviathan.name: Leviathan
leviathan.text: The creature made by God supplies the creation focus (Psalm 104:26; Job 41); judgment imagery in Isaiah is a distinct use. Creature and poetic monster imagery In that day, the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish leviathan, the fleeing serpent, and leviathan, the twisted serpent; and he will kill the dragon that is in the sea. Isaiah 27:1 · World English Bible There the ships go, and leviathan, whom you formed to play there. Psalm 104:26 · World English Bible Leviathan appears both as a creature God formed and as a monster overcome by divine power. Job stresses human inability to master it; these passages do not explicitly identify Leviathan as Satan or name it a demon.

rahab.name: Rahab in the sea imagery
rahab.text: The sea-victory image accompanies deliverance of the redeemed (Isaiah 51:9–11). Poetic monster image Awake, awake, put on strength, arm of the LORD! Awake, as in the days of old, the generations of ancient times. Isn’t it you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the monster? Isaiah 51:9 · World English Bible Rahab appears in a poetic appeal to God’s past victory, immediately connected with the sea becoming a path for the redeemed. The passage supplies an image of defeated opposition rather than a named demon’s biography. Read in context: Isaiah 51:10–11 Verse references: Rahab in the sea imagery

pharaoh-monster.name: Pharaoh as the great monster
pharaoh-monster.text: The monster image addresses Pharaoh's pride and coming judgment (Ezekiel 29). Image for a human ruler Speak and say, ‘The Lord Yahweh says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great monster that lies in the middle of his rivers, that has said, ‘My river is my own, and I have made it for myself.’ Ezekiel 29:3 · World English Bible Classic The prophecy expressly addresses Pharaoh, using a river-monster image for his pride and coming humiliation. Its stated human target prevents treating every occurrence of monster language as a literal demon description. Read in context: Ezekiel 29:2–6, 9–10 Verse references: Pharaoh as the great monster

behemoth.name: Behemoth
behemoth.text: God explicitly presents Behemoth as a creature he made (Job 40:15). Powerful creature in divine speech “See now behemoth, which I made as well as you. He eats grass as an ox. Job 40:15 · World English Bible God presents Behemoth to Job as a creature of formidable strength that God has made. The account describes its feeding, body, and habitat without calling it an evil spirit or placing it under Satan. Read in context: Job 40:16–24 Verse references: Behemoth

daniel-beasts.name: Daniel’s four beasts
daniel-beasts.text: The vision is interpreted as kings and kingdoms to come (Daniel 7). Symbols of kings and kingdoms ‘These great animals, which are four, are four kings, who will arise out of the earth. Daniel 7:17 · World English Bible The interpretation inside the vision identifies the beasts with kings and the fourth beast with a kingdom. Their terrifying forms portray earthly rule that is judged before the kingdom is given to the saints. Read in context: Daniel 7:18, 23–27 Verse references: Daniel’s four beasts

revelation-beasts.name: The beasts in Revelation
revelation-beasts.text: The entry describes blasphemous, deceptive and persecuting power in Revelation. Visionary images of opposing power The beast which I saw was like a leopard, and his feet were like those of a bear, and his mouth like the mouth of a lion. The dragon gave him his power, his throne, and great authority. Revelation 13:2 · World English Bible The sea beast receives authority from the dragon, while another beast promotes its worship and deceives the earth. Revelation’s later interpretation connects heads and horns with kings; the beasts remain distinguishable from the dragon who empowers them. Read in context: Revelation 13:11–18 ; Revelation 17:9–14 ; Revelation 20:10 Verse references: The beasts

abaddon-apollyon.name: ✦ Abaddon and Apollyon
abaddon-apollyon.text: The angel's named role belongs to a bounded judgment (Revelation 9:11); no identity with Satan is assumed. Named angel in an apocalyptic judgment They have over them as king the angel of the abyss. His name in Hebrew is “Abaddon”, but in Greek, he has the name “Apollyon”. Revelation 9:11 · World English Bible These are the two names Revelation gives to the angel ruling the locusts from the abyss. The passage assigns him a role in a bounded judgment; it does not explicitly identify him with Satan, Michael, or another named figure. Read in context: Revelation 9:1–11 Verse references: Abaddon and Apollyon

death-hades.name: Death and Hades
death-hades.text: The figures belong to Revelation's judgment imagery and are later judged themselves. Personified powers and the realm of the dead And behold, a pale horse, and the name of he who sat on it was Death. Hades followed with him. Authority over one fourth of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and by the wild animals of the earth was given to him. Revelation 6:8 · World English Bible Revelation personifies Death as a rider and Hades as his follower. Both later surrender their dead and are cast into the lake of fire; this imagery should not be converted without explanation into two ordinary demon names. Read in context: Revelation 20:13–14 Verse references: Death and Hades

seven-spirits.name: Seven Spirits of God: a debated symbolic designation
seven-spirits.text: This visionary designation has more than one stated interpretation. Orange marks the vision without deciding between the Spirit's fullness and angelic spirits. symbolic expression with disputed referent I saw in the middle of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the middle of the elders, a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God, sent out into all the earth. Revelation 5:6 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) Revelation presents seven Spirits before God’s throne and identifies them with the Lamb’s seven eyes sent throughout the earth. One major interpretation understands the number symbolically as the ful

wormwood.name: Wormwood
wormwood.text: The named star belongs to the bitter-water judgment (Revelation 8:10–11). Named star in a vision The name of the star is “Wormwood.” One third of the waters became wormwood. Many people died from the waters, because they were made bitter. Revelation 8:11 · World English Bible The falling star’s name is linked with the bitter waters in the trumpet judgment. This passage calls it a star, without explicitly naming it an angel or demon. Read in context: Revelation 8:10 Verse references: Wormwood

names-that-need-care.name: Names that need care
names-that-need-care.text: Read this category on its own → Mammon · Azazel and the scapegoat · Lucifer and the day-star · The king of Tyre and the covering cherub image · Lilith and the night creature

mammon.name: Mammon
mammon.text: Jesus warns against wealth becoming a rival master; the entry does not assert a demon's identity. New Testament personification of wealth No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon. Matthew 6:24 · King James Version In Jesus’ teaching, mammon refers to wealth and is personified as a rival master demanding allegiance. Matthew places the warning after teaching about earthly and heavenly treasure. Luke connects mammon with stewardship, faithfulness, and true riches. The central issue is loyalty to God and the use of possessions. These passages do not identify Mammon as

azazel.name: Azazel and the scapegoat
azazel.text: The term belongs to instructions for the two-goat rite (Leviticus 16); its disputed identity remains qualified. Translation-sensitive ritual term with debated identity And Aaron shall cast lots upon the two goats: one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for Azazel. Leviticus 16:8 · JPS 1917 And Aaron shall cast lots upon the two goats; one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for the scapegoat. Leviticus 16:8 · King James Version And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land which is cut off; and he shall let go the goat in the wilderness. Leviticus 16:22 · JPS 1917 JPS retains Azazel from the Hebrew while the KJV uses scapegoat; both readings belong to the same two-goat r

lucifer.name: Lucifer and the day-star
lucifer.text: The quoted day-star language occurs in a taunt against Babylon's king (Isaiah 14); it is not an unqualified naming of Satan. Translation wording in a royal taunt How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations! Isaiah 14:12 · King James Version How art thou fallen from heaven, O day-star, son of the morning! How art thou cut down to the ground, that didst cast lots over the nations! Isaiah 14:12 · JPS 1917 Isaiah introduces the speech as a taunt against Babylon’s king and later asks whether this is the man who shook kingdoms. The verse does not explicitly give Lucifer as Satan’s personal name; further identif

king-tyre.name: The king of Tyre and the covering cherub image
king-tyre.text: The lament addresses a ruler's pride and expulsion (Ezekiel 28); further identifications remain interpretation. Royal lament with Eden and cherub imagery You were the anointed cherub who covers. Then I set you up on the holy mountain of God. You have walked up and down in the middle of the stones of fire. Ezekiel 28:14 · World English Bible Classic The lament expressly addresses the king of Tyre, while portraying Eden, a cherub, pride, and expulsion. The surrounding oracle calls the ruler human; identifying the lament’s figure with Satan goes beyond an explicit identification in this chapter. Read in context: Ezekiel 28:2, 9, 12–17 Verse references: The king of Tyre and the covering cherub i

lilith.name: Lilith and the night creature
lilith.text: The term occurs in Edom's desolation poem (Isaiah 34); the color does not assert a later demon biography. Translation-sensitive term in desolation poetry And the wild-cats shall meet with the jackals, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; yea, the night-monster shall repose there, and shall find her a place of rest. Isaiah 34:14 · JPS 1917 The Hebrew term lilith appears among the inhabitants of ruined Edom; JPS renders it night-monster and the World English Bible uses night creature. The verse gives no family history, relationship to Adam, or account of a named demon’s actions beyond this scene. Read in context: Isaiah 34:5, 11–15 ; Isaiah 34:14 Verse references: Lilith and the night creatu

tobit.name: Raphael and Asmodeus in Tobit
tobit.text: Read this category on its own → Tobit is included in Catholic and Orthodox biblical collections. It is not part of every biblical canon and is outside the present Saints.Bible seventy-book collection. The quotations below link to the biblical text itself. Raphael · Asmodeus or Asmodaeus

raphael.name: ✦ Raphael
raphael.text: Raphael's ministry brings healing and help to Tobit's household. Named angel I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels which present the prayers of the saints and go in before the glory of the Holy One. Tobit 12:15 · World English Bible Classic Raphael identifies himself as an angel sent by God after helping Tobit’s family. His work includes presenting prayers, healing, and binding the demon troubling Sarah; this verse calls him an angel without using the title archangel. Tobit belongs to Catholic and Orthodox biblical collections and is outside the present Saints.Bible seventy-book collection. Read in context: Tobit 3:16–17 ; Tobit 8:3 ; Tobit 12:12–18 Verse references: Raphael

asmodeus.name: ✕ Asmodeus or Asmodaeus
asmodeus.text: Tobit explicitly describes the spirit's harmful opposition and its restraint. Named evil spirit because that she had been given to seven husbands, and Asmodaeus the evil spirit killed them, before they had lain with her. And they said to her, “Do you not know that you strangle your husbands? You have had already seven husbands, and you haven’t borne the name of any one of them.” Tobit 3:8 · World English Bible Classic Tobit attributes the deaths of Sarah’s husbands to this evil spirit, while reporting the unjust blame directed at her. God sends Raphael to bring relief, and the demon is bound; the narrative provides no broader catalogue of his supposed powers. Tobit belongs to Catholic and Or

egyptian-plagues.name: Egypt’s gods and the ten plagues
egyptian-plagues.text: Read this category on its own → Biblical account with clearly labelled historical comparisons Exodus describes judgment on Egypt’s gods (Exodus 12:12; Numbers 33:4), but does not name a different god for each plague. These comparisons distinguish documented Egyptian beliefs from proposed interpretations of the biblical story. They are not ten established identifications. Egyptian deities shared attributes and changed across periods and places. The Egyptian roles described below are historical evidence; identifying a particular deity as a plague’s intended target is an interpretation. A strong association between a deity and an animal or natural force does not prove that Exodus targets that d

plagues-biblical-foundation.name: What Scripture explicitly says
plagues-biblical-foundation.text: For I will go through the land of Egypt in that night, and will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and animal. I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt. I am Yahweh. Exodus 12:12 · World English Bible Classic God announces judgment against all the gods of Egypt in the instructions for Passover and the impending death of the firstborn. while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom Yahweh had struck among them. Yahweh also executed judgments on their gods. Numbers 33:4 · World English Bible Classic This retrospective account of Israel's departure connects the death of Egypt's firstborn with judgment on Egypt's gods. The verse begins with a lowerc

plague-1.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. Moses and Aaron did so, as Yahweh commanded; and he lifted up the rod, and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh, and in the sight of his servants; and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood. Exodus 7:20 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: The river's waters turn to blood. Its fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink its water. Account: Exodus 7:14–25. God states in verse 17 that Pharaoh is to know that he is Yahweh. Egypt's water supply is struck, but Pharaoh refuses to t

plague-2.name: 2. Frogs
plague-2.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt; and the frogs came up, and covered the land of Egypt. Exodus 8:6 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Frogs cover the land and enter the Egyptians' houses, bedrooms, ovens, and kneading troughs. Account: Exodus 8:1–15. Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron to appeal to Yahweh for relief. Moses connects the appointed time of the frogs' removal with knowing that no one is like Yahweh. Pharaoh hardens his heart when relief comes (verses 8–15). Historical proposal: Heqet, also sp

plague-3.name: 3. Lice
plague-3.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. The magicians tried with their enchantments to produce lice, but they couldn’t. There were lice on man, and on animal. Exodus 8:18 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Aaron strikes the dust of the earth, and lice afflict people and animals throughout Egypt. Account: Exodus 8:16–19. Egypt's magicians cannot reproduce the sign. They acknowledge God's involvement, but Pharaoh still will not listen. The passage contrasts their inability with God's power. WEB Classic uses the word lice for this plague. Historical proposal: N

plague-4.name: 4. Swarms of flies
plague-4.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. Yahweh did so; and there came grievous swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh, and into his servants’ houses. In all the land of Egypt the land was corrupted by reason of the swarms of flies. Exodus 8:24 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Swarms of flies enter Egyptian houses and ruin the land, while Goshen is set apart. Account: Exodus 8:20–32. God explicitly sets apart Goshen, where his people live. This distinction is a sign intended to make Pharaoh recognize Yahweh's presence and authority on the earth (verses 2

plague-5.name: 5. Disease on livestock
plague-5.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. Yahweh did that thing on the next day; and all the livestock of Egypt died, but of the livestock of the children of Israel, not one died. Exodus 9:6 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: A severe pestilence strikes Egypt's livestock; Israel's livestock are spared. Account: Exodus 9:1–7. The warning in verse 3 concerns Egypt's livestock in the field. God announces both a set time and a distinction between Egypt's livestock and Israel's. Pharaoh verifies that Israel's livestock were spared, yet remains stubborn (verses 4–7)

plague-6.name: 6. Boils
plague-6.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. They took ashes of the furnace, and stood before Pharaoh; and Moses sprinkled it up toward the sky; and it became boils and blisters breaking out on man and on animal. Exodus 9:10 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Boils and blisters break out on people and animals after Moses scatters furnace ashes toward the sky. Account: Exodus 9:8–12. The judgment reaches human and animal bodies. The magicians are themselves afflicted and cannot stand before Moses (verse 11). Those who had attempted to rival the signs cannot shield

plague-7.name: 7. Hail and lightning
plague-7.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. So there was very severe hail, and lightning mixed with the hail, such as had not been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. Exodus 9:24 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: An unprecedented hailstorm strikes people, animals, crops, and trees in the field; Goshen has no hail. Account: Exodus 9:13–35. God declares that there is no one like him in all the earth. His warning provides a way to shelter people and livestock, and some of Pharaoh's servants heed it (verses 14–21). Moses explains that the ending of t

plague-8.name: 8. Locusts
plague-8.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. For they covered the surface of the whole earth, so that the land was darkened, and they ate every herb of the land, and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left. There remained nothing green, either tree or herb of the field, through all the land of Egypt. Exodus 10:15 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Locusts cover Egypt and consume the vegetation and fruit that the hail left behind. Account: Exodus 10:1–20. God confronts Pharaoh's refusal to humble himself, while explaining that these signs are to be reco

plague-9.name: 9. Darkness
plague-9.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days. Exodus 10:22 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: Thick darkness lasts three days in Egypt, while the Israelites have light in their dwellings. Account: Exodus 10:21–29. Egypt is immobilized by darkness, while the Israelites have light (verse 23). Pharaoh offers a conditional release that would leave their livestock behind. Moses insists that they must leave with what they need to serve Yahweh (verses 24–2

plague-10.name: 10. Death of the firstborn
plague-10.text: This plague is presented as judgment in the cited Exodus account. Proposed Egyptian-deity comparisons remain labeled interpretations, not certain identities. At midnight, Yahweh struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of livestock. Exodus 12:29 · World English Bible Classic Biblical significance: The firstborn die throughout Egypt, including Pharaoh's firstborn and the firstborn of livestock. God provides Passover instructions for the protection of Israel's households. Account: Exodus 11:1–10; 12:1–32. This is the setting in which God expressly announces ju

plagues-significance.name: Why the plagues matter
plagues-significance.text: The plagues reveal who Yahweh is. Egypt is to recognize him, and Israel is to remember his works and teach them to later generations. They expose the limits of Pharaoh and his magicians, confront Pharaoh's refusal to release God's people, and culminate in Israel's deliverance. Passover establishes an enduring remembrance of that rescue. Sources: Exodus 7:4–5 ; Exodus 10:1–3 ; Exodus 12:14, 26–27, 51 Verse references: Why the plagues matter Reference scope for this study This is an event or interpretive study. plagues-historical-limits.name: Scholarly interpretation and limits
plagues-historical-limits.text: Ziony Zevit discusses deity comparisons sympathetically but acknowledges missing candidates and warns that the supporting Egyptian evidence comes from different periods and places. It does not establish a single contemporary ten-deity scheme. Sources: Ziony Zevit: Three Ways to Look at the Ten Plagues Kerry Muhlestein emphasizes a collective confrontation with Pharaoh’s divine kingship and maintenance of order rather than ten isolated deity defeats. This is an interpretation of the narrative in Egyptian context, not independent verification of the events. father-biblical.name: Biblical names and titles
father-biblical.text: The Hebrew Scriptures preserve the divine name YHWH alongside titles such as El, Elohim, Adonai, and God Most High. Other expressions describe God’s character and action. Some familiar YHWH combinations actually name an altar, a place, a ruler, or a city; each entry identifies what its passage names. These shared divine designations are gathered here for navigation, without assigning them exclusively to the Father. yhwh-yahweh.name: YHWH / Yahweh
yhwh-yahweh.text: This entry studies a name or designation of God in the Father/Creator section. Shared titles are not restricted to the Father in every passage. divine name or title God said moreover to Moses, “You shall tell the children of Israel this, ‘Yahweh, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is my memorial to all generations. Exodus 3:15 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) YHWH is the four-consonant personal name of Israel’s God, often called the Tetragrammaton. The familiar rendering is “I AM WHO I AM”; the Hebrew also permits the future-oriented “I will be who I will be.” The same verb appears in the promise to be with Moses in Exodus 3:12. el.text: This entry studies a name or designation of God in the Father/Creator section. Shared titles are not restricted to the Father in every passage. divine name or title God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent. Has he said, and he won’t do it? Or has he spoken, and he won’t make it good? Numbers 23:19 · World English Bible Classic (WEB) El is a Hebrew word for “God” or “god,” and it also appears in combinations such as El Elyon and El Shaddai. Here it refers to Israel’s God in Balaam’s oracle. Balak wants Israel cursed, but Balaam declares that God’s blessing cannot be overturned by human pressure. father-history.name: Historical forms and interpretations
father-history.text: A written name, a reconstructed pronunciation, and a translation convention are different kinds of evidence. YHWH is the preserved Hebrew consonantal form. Yahweh is the usual scholarly reconstruction, with acknowledged uncertainty. Jehovah is a later established form of that same name, and LORD is an English rendering convention. Yahuah is documented here as a modern advocated pronunciation, with its community’s claims distinguished from independent linguistic evidence. son-history.name: Historical forms and interpretations
son-history.text: Jesus, Greek Iēsous, and the related Hebrew forms Yeshua and Yehoshua belong to the name’s language history; they do not identify different persons. Interpretive history also matters for titles. Isaiah 9:6 is traditionally read by Christians in relation to Jesus, while scholars debate aspects of its original royal setting and the wording of its titles. The entry distinguishes the biblical text from its later application. holy-spirit-biblical.text: Holy Spirit, Spirit of God, Spirit of Christ, Spirit of truth, and Spirit of adoption describe the Spirit in different biblical contexts. John identifies the promised Counselor with the Holy Spirit; Paul connects the Spirit with life in Christ and the cry to God as Father. These are related designations and descriptions, not a list of separate spirits. Translation differences and the context of each expression are kept visible. holy-spirit-history.name: Historical forms and interpretations
holy-spirit-history.text: Holy Ghost is an older English rendering of the expression also translated Holy Spirit. Paraclete represents a Greek term translated Counselor, Helper, Comforter, or Advocate. Other expressions require interpretive care: the referent of “eternal Spirit” in Hebrews 9:14 is discussed, and Revelation’s seven Spirits have been read as the Spirit’s fullness or as heavenly angelic spirits. The entries distinguish these readings instead of treating every expression as a settled personal name. terminology-title.text: A starting point for the language of Scripture, Christian belief, and biblical research. 49 introductory entries · Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Latin context · Sources beside each term Study Guides / Christian Terminology & Lexicon Explore a term, read its source, then return to the passage. These concise entries distinguish a word’s possible meanings from its use in a particular text. They also identify theological language whose meaning depends on a Christian tradition.

how-to-use.name: Two ways of understanding a word
how-to-use.text: Christian terminology explains concepts used in teaching, worship, and interpretation. A language lexicon investigates words, their grammatical forms, and their possible senses in actual texts. This page offers an introductory selection of both. It is not an exhaustive original-language lexicon. Definitions are editorial summaries; biblical passages illustrate usage, while named church sources document particular theological formulations.

term-acrostic.name: Acrostic
term-acrostic.text: Literary terminology · Alphabetic form in Hebrew poetry An alphabetic acrostic arranges successive lines, verses, or stanzas according to the letters of an alphabet. Psalm 119 is a clear biblical example: its twenty-two stanzas follow the Hebrew alphabet, and each stanza contains eight verses beginning with the same Hebrew letter. The USCCB’s note describes this structure; the Hebrew text lets a reader inspect it directly. In Psalm 119:1–8 the verse openings use aleph; verses 9–16 use beth. The accompanying English translation does not reproduce those initial letters. A translation may signal the pattern through headings even when its own wording does not form an acrostic. term-anagogy-four-senses.name: Anagogy / Four Senses of Scripture
term-anagogy-four-senses.text: Aliases: anagogy, anagogical, four senses of Scripture · Catholic interpretive terminology In the Catholic Catechism, anagogy or anagogical reading considers the eternal significance of biblical realities and events. It belongs to a framework that distinguishes the literal sense from three spiritual senses (§§115–119): Literal: the meaning communicated by the text, established through careful interpretation (§116). Allegorical: events understood in relation to Christ (§117). Moral: events read as guidance for just action (§117). term-antiphon.name: Antiphon
term-antiphon.text: Liturgical terminology · Usage depends on the worship tradition An antiphon is a short liturgical text or refrain, often associated with a psalm. In the Saint Helena Breviary , it is said or sung before and after a psalm or group of psalms; its wording may come from Scripture or another source and reflect the season or commemoration. This describes the practice of the Order of Saint Helena, an Episcopal religious community, rather than a rule shared by all Christians. term-baptism.name: Baptism
term-baptism.text: Greek: βάπτισμα (baptisma) A Christian rite involving water and entry into the life of discipleship. In Romans 6, Paul connects baptism with sharing in Christ’s death and resurrection and living differently afterward. Christian traditions differ over whom to baptize, how to administer baptism, and how to explain its relationship to salvation. Matthew speaks of the poor in spirit and those who hunger and thirst for righteousness; Luke addresses the poor and hungry and follows the blessings with corresponding woes (6:24–26). term-chiasmus.name: Chiasmus / Chiasm
term-chiasmus.text: Literary and rhetorical terminology · Reversed correspondence Chiasmus describes a reversed arrangement of corresponding ideas or grammatical structures, often represented as A–B–B–A. Terminology varies: Gideon O. Burton’s Silva Rhetoricae distinguishes chiasmus from antimetabole, the narrower repetition of the same words in reverse order, while noting that the names sometimes overlap. Isaiah 5:20 offers a small, directly checkable example of reversed wording: evil/good, then good/evil; darkness/light, then light/darkness. Burton lists this under antimetabole. term-christ-messiah.text: Greek: Χριστός (Christos) · Hebrew: מָשִׁיחַ “Christ” and “Messiah” connect Greek and Hebrew language for an anointed person. In John 1:41, Andrew identifies Jesus as the Messiah. In Christian usage, calling Jesus “Christ” expresses a claim about his identity and mission, rather than supplying a family name. Earlier Hebrew occurrences of the word must be read in their own settings. term-codex.name: Codex / Codices
term-codex.text: Manuscript and book-history terminology · Plural: codices A codex is a book made from folded sheets gathered and bound together, rather than a continuous roll. The term identifies a physical format, not a particular translation, biblical canon, or level of textual authority. The University of Missouri’s book-history glossary describes the construction of this form. The Codex Sinaiticus project explains that early Christian books could be made from papyrus, while Codex Sinaiticus itself uses parchment, prepared animal skin. term-colophon.name: Colophon
term-colophon.text: Manuscript and book-history terminology · Production note A colophon is a note, commonly at the end of a manuscript or book, which may identify its scribe or printer, date, place of production, patron, or title. Hill Museum & Manuscript Library notes that some colophons also describe historical events or ask readers to pray for the scribe. Their contents and conventions vary. Study caution: A copying note is evidence to evaluate, not automatically the date or author of the biblical work being copied. term-covenant.name: Covenant
term-covenant.text: Hebrew: בְּרִית · Greek: διαθήκη (diathēkē) A solemn relationship expressed through promises and commitments. Genesis 17 describes God’s covenant with Abraham and his descendants, including a sign and obligations. At the Last Supper in Luke, Jesus speaks of a new covenant in his blood. Each covenant should be read within its own narrative and historical setting. term-doxology.name: Doxology
term-doxology.text: Christian literary and liturgical terminology · A form of praise, not the name of only one hymn A doxology is an expression of praise that ascribes glory to God. Jude 24–25 offers a biblical example: it praises God’s ability to preserve believers and concludes by attributing glory, majesty, dominion, and power to God. Calling this ending a doxology describes its function; it does not mean the English term appears in the passage. Churches also use the word for later prayers or hymns.
