term-ekklesia.name: Ekklēsia
term-ekklesia.text: Greek: ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) A Greek word for an assembly, used in the New Testament for Christian congregations and the Church. It can also describe a civic gathering, as in Acts 19. Its meaning depends on the people and setting in view; deriving a complete theology from “called-out ones” overlooks this range of actual usage. Read the sources: Acts 19:32, 39, 41 (World English Bible) · Mounce: Greek headword, Matthew 16:18 and other textual examples Back to the term index ↑

term-eucharist.name: Eucharist
term-eucharist.text: Greek: εὐχαριστία (eucharistia) A name for the Christian celebration also called Holy Communion or the Lord’s Supper. The name draws on Greek language for thanksgiving. Its biblical setting includes Jesus sharing bread and the cup with his disciples. Churches differ in their explanations of Christ’s presence, sacramental effects, and who may receive Communion. Read the sources: Luke 22:14–20 (World English Bible) · Catholic explanation of the names: Catechism §§1328–1329 · Mounce: Greek headword Back to the term index ↑

term-favor.name: Favor / Favour
term-favor.text: English spelling variants · Greek example: χάρις (charis) Kindly regard, gracious acceptance, or goodwill shown toward someone. The exact sense depends on who gives and receives it. In Luke 2:52, Jesus grows in “favour with God and man” (KJV); the World English Bible Classic spells the word “favor.” This is not the sensory word savor / savour . The Greek charis in Luke 2:52 can express favor; elsewhere its range includes grace, a gift, or thanks. Do not transfer every possible sense into a single passage. For the related theological discussion, see Grace / Charis . Read the sources: Luke 2:52 (KJV) · Luke 2:52 (WEB Classic) · Mounce: charis and biblical occurrences Back to the term index ↑

term-flavor.name: Flavor / Flavour
term-flavor.text: Modern English taste wording · See Savor / Savour Taste or the distinctive quality perceived in tasting. This is a genuine translation choice in some Bible editions, not the wording of every Bible: Matthew 5:13 has salt losing its “savour” in the KJV and its “flavor” in the World English Bible Classic. Here both express the loss of salt’s taste. “Flavor” should not replace every biblical occurrence of “savour,” which can instead refer to aroma or, as a verb, a person’s mindset. Read the sources: Matthew 5:13 (KJV) · Matthew 5:13 (WEB Classic) · Mounce: mōrainō in the salt saying Back to the term index ↑

term-grace-charis.name: Grace / Charis
term-grace-charis.text: Greek: χάρις (charis) Grace names God’s generous favor and gift in Christian teaching. Ephesians 2:8–10 presents salvation as God’s gift and places good works within the life that follows. The Greek word charis has a wider range, including favor and thanks, so its meaning in any verse requires attention to that verse’s context. Read the sources: Ephesians 2:8–10 (World English Bible) · Mounce: Greek headword and range Back to the term index ↑

term-hallelujah.name: Hallelujah / Alleluia
term-hallelujah.text: Hebrew praise expression retained in Greek: ἁλληλουϊά (hallēlouia) An acclamation calling for praise of Yah, a short form of the divine name. Psalm 150 begins and ends with this praise language; the World English Bible Classic renders it “Praise Yah!” Revelation 19:1–6 retains “Hallelujah” amid heavenly worship celebrating God’s judgment and reign. “Hallelujah” and “Alleluia” are alternative forms encountered in English Bibles and Christian worship. The expression is not a separate personal name for God and should not be counted as a standalone occurrence of “Yah” merely because that name forms part of it. Follow the chosen edition’s actual wording when comparing occurrences. Read the source

term-hapax-legomenon.name: Hapax legomenon
term-hapax-legomenon.text: Research terminology · Plural: hapax legomena A word attested only once in a specified body of texts. The scope matters: once in one biblical book is not the same as once in the Hebrew Bible, the Greek New Testament, or all surviving literature in that language. A single surviving occurrence does not by itself show how common the word was in everyday speech. Example: Gary A. Rendsburg identifies Hebrew gopher , the wood named in Genesis 6:14, as a biblical hapax. The World English Bible Classic retains “gopher wood.” A proposed identification of the wood is an interpretation requiring further evidence; the label hapax does not identify the tree. term-hesed.name: Hesed / Chesed
term-hesed.text: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) · Contextual kindness, mercy, and loyalty A Hebrew word whose uses include kindness between people and God’s loving kindness toward his people. The Brown–Driver–Briggs lexicon distinguishes several contexts rather than supplying one English equivalent for every occurrence. In Ruth 3:10, the World English Bible Classic renders the word as “kindness,” within Boaz’s response to Ruth’s concern for her family. Some passages explicitly connect ḥesed with covenant. Elinoar Bareket’s study emphasizes relational obligations and reciprocal loyalty in texts such as Deuteronomy 7:9 and 1 Samuel 20:8. That is an attributed scholarly interpretation of selected contexts, not a rule th

term-hosanna.name: Hosanna
term-hosanna.text: Greek: ὡσαννά (hōsanna) · A Hebrew plea for salvation used as an acclamation “Hosanna” carries the sense of an appeal to save or help. Psalm 118:25–26 places a plea for rescue beside a blessing on the one who comes in God’s name. In Matthew 21:9, the crowds acclaim Jesus as Son of David with Hosanna and the blessing from that psalm. The expression’s force in the Gospel scene includes praise and welcome, not only a dictionary gloss of “save now.” Conversely, treating it as a generic synonym for “hooray” loses its scriptural setting. Keep the original plea, the psalm’s blessing, and the Gospel’s presentation of Jesus together without making the expression itself a personal title. Read the sour

term-inclusio.name: Inclusio
term-inclusio.text: Literary terminology · Framing repetition An inclusio is a framing pattern in which corresponding wording or themes near the beginning and end help mark a literary unit. Unlike the reversed sequence described under chiasmus, the emphasis is on the surrounding frame. In her Working Preacher commentary, Nancy deClaissé-Walford identifies an inclusio in Psalm 104: the call to bless God in verse 1 returns in verse 35. The WEB Classic renders the repeated words “Bless Yahweh, my soul.” The final verse also includes “Praise Yah!”; the framing phrase need not be the last words on the page. Study practice: Compare the proposed opening and closing in the same edition, then read what lies between them

term-incarnation.name: Incarnation
term-incarnation.text: The teaching that the Son of God truly became human in Jesus Christ. John 1:14 supplies its central biblical language: the Word became flesh and lived among human beings. The Catholic formulation cited here emphasizes real human existence, not simply a divine appearance, and connects Jesus’ human life with God’s saving work. Read the sources: John 1:14–18 (World English Bible) · Catholic doctrinal formulation: Catechism §§461–463 Back to the term index ↑

term-kerygma.name: Kērygma / Proclamation
term-kerygma.text: Greek: κήρυγμα (kērygma) A Greek noun for proclamation or preaching, including the message proclaimed. Matthew 12:41 uses it of Jonah’s preaching to Nineveh. In 1 Corinthians 15:14, Paul says that Christian preaching would be empty if Christ had not been raised; the surrounding argument identifies the death, burial, resurrection, and appearances of Christ as central to the message he received and handed on. In Christian discussion, kerygma often points to the proclamation of the gospel. The biblical word is not, however, a technical label for one fixed later outline wherever it occurs: Jonah’s preaching and Paul’s resurrection argument have different immediate settings. Identify who proclaim

term-koinonia.name: Koinōnia
term-koinonia.text: Greek: κοινωνία (koinōnia) · Fellowship, participation, sharing A Greek noun used for fellowship or participation, and in some contexts for a material contribution. The World English Bible Classic uses “fellowship” in Acts 2:42, “sharing” in 1 Corinthians 10:16, and “contribution” in Romans 15:26. The last passage concerns aid for poor believers in Jerusalem, showing why a single English gloss does not fit every setting. Mounce’s lexical entry connects these uses with sharing or association. Its range of senses is not a list of meanings to insert simultaneously into every verse. In 1 Corinthians 10:16–21, Paul’s discussion of the cup, bread, and rival tables supplies the context; the noun by

term-lexicon-lemma.name: Lexicon / Lemma
term-lexicon-lemma.text: A lexicon is a dictionary used to investigate words and their meanings. In language study, a lemma is the headword under which related grammatical forms are listed. Finding a lemma is the beginning of study: compare possible senses, the sentence’s grammar, and the wider passage before choosing a meaning for a particular occurrence. Read the sources: University of Cambridge: Greek Lexicon and contextual meanings · TEI Consortium: lemma, note distinguishing the language-study sense Back to the term index ↑

term-logos.name: Logos
term-logos.text: Greek: λόγος (logos) A Greek word with uses such as word, message, speech, or account. John’s Gospel gives it a distinctive theological role: the Word was with God, was God, and became flesh. This use informs Christian reflection on Jesus, but it should not be imported into every occurrence of logos elsewhere. Read the sources: John 1:1–18 (World English Bible) · Mounce: Greek headword and other uses Back to the term index ↑

term-maranatha.name: Maranatha
term-maranatha.text: Aramaic expression preserved in the Greek New Testament · Word division affects interpretation An Aramaic expression in the closing greetings of 1 Corinthians 16:22. The World English Bible Classic translates it “Come, Lord!” and identifies Maranatha in its note. Read as marana tha , it is an appeal for the Lord to come; read with a different division, maran atha , it can be understood as “Our Lord has come.” The New American Bible, Revised Edition note explains these two readings and favors the prayer for Christ’s return, comparing Revelation 22:20. This is a genuine linguistic and interpretive distinction, not a license to combine both renderings as if the phrase stated them simultaneously

term-masoretic-text.name: Masoretic Text / MT
term-masoretic-text.text: Jewish biblical transmission tradition · Not a translation or an original autograph The Masoretic Text names a Jewish tradition of preserving and reading the Hebrew Bible. The Masoretes, generations of scribe-scholars, recorded inherited reading traditions with vowel and cantillation signs and compiled notes intended to safeguard the text. These signs and notes accompany the consonantal wording; they are not an additional biblical book. ANU Museum’s account of Codex Sassoon distinguishes the brief Masorah parva notes alongside the biblical text from the fuller Masorah magna notes in the upper and lower margins. The Aleppo Codex is another important manuscript witness: Cambridge’s Genizah Res

term-merism.name: Merism
term-merism.text: Literary terminology · A whole expressed through contrasting parts A merism names parts or extremes to express an encompassing whole. In biblical study, this often means reading a pair in relation to the wider claim being made, rather than treating the pair as an exhaustive list of isolated items. The NET Bible’s note on Genesis 1:1 identifies “the heavens and the earth” as a phrase often interpreted this way: the created universe as a whole. This is an explicitly attributed interpretation, not a separate Hebrew word meaning “merism.” In Psalm 139:2–3, sitting down and rising up, going and lying down, belong to the psalm’s description of God knowing all the speaker’s ways. Study caution: Not

term-metonymy.name: Metonymy
term-metonymy.text: Literary and linguistic terminology · Naming by association Metonymy refers to something by naming an associated person, object, place, or attribute. Gideon O. Burton’s Silva Rhetoricae illustrates the figure with a crown standing for the authority associated with it. The link is an association in context, not simply a claim that two things look alike. Biblical example: In Luke 16:29–31, “Moses and the prophets” names the scriptural testimony that the rich man’s brothers already have and should heed. Reading the names as a reference to that testimony explains the argument without imagining that the brothers physically possess those people. Identify the association before drawing a theologica

term-metanoia.name: Metanoia
term-metanoia.text: Greek: μετάνοια (metanoia) A Greek word commonly translated “repentance.” In Luke 3, John connects repentance with changed conduct, including generosity and honest treatment of others. In this setting it involves a reorientation of life toward God, rather than merely feeling regret or replacing one opinion with another. Read the sources: Luke 3:3, 8–14 (World English Bible) · Mounce: Greek headword and occurrences Back to the term index ↑

term-palimpsest.name: Palimpsest
term-palimpsest.text: Manuscript-study terminology · Erased and overwritten text A palimpsest is a manuscript whose earlier writing has been erased so that the material can be used for a new text. The earlier layer is often called the undertext and the later writing the overtext. These layers must be identified separately rather than read as one continuous composition. Biblical example: The Early Manuscripts Electronic Library’s Codex Zacynthius project describes an erased seventh- or eighth-century Greek copy of Luke with extracts from early Christian theologians beside the biblical text. Its spectral-imaging work illustrates how manuscript study can distinguish and recover an earlier layer. Enhanced images do n

term-parallelism.name: Parallelism
term-parallelism.text: Literary terminology · Corresponding lines in biblical poetry Poetic parallelism places corresponding words, images, or clauses alongside one another. The next line may reinforce, contrast with, or develop the first. It should not automatically be dismissed as saying exactly the same thing twice. Tim Mackie’s BibleProject class notes describe comparison, complement, contrast, and sequence as ways such lines relate. Read the pattern: Psalm 19:1 pairs the heavens declaring God’s glory with the expanse showing his handiwork. Proverbs 10:1 contrasts a wise son’s effect on his father with a foolish son’s effect on his mother. These examples invite attention both to the correspondences and to what

term-parousia.name: Parousia
term-parousia.text: Greek: παρουσία (parousia) · Presence, arrival, or coming according to context A Greek noun that can describe someone’s presence or arrival. In Philippians 2:12, Paul contrasts his presence with his absence. In 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18, the Lord’s coming is the setting for the resurrection of believers who have died and the community’s hope of being with him. Christian theology commonly uses Parousia for Christ’s awaited coming. That specialized usage should not be read into every biblical occurrence of the noun: 1 Corinthians 16:17 uses it for the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. The word itself does not establish a timetable or settle differing Christian interpretations of en

term-pneuma-ruach.name: Pneuma / Ruach
term-pneuma-ruach.text: Greek: πνεῦμα (pneuma) · Hebrew: רוּחַ Greek pneuma and Hebrew ruach can refer to wind, breath, or spirit, depending on context. John 3:8 draws on the relationship between wind and Spirit; Ezekiel 37 moves through imagery of breath, winds, and God’s spirit. These overlapping meanings enrich the passages without making every occurrence a reference to the Holy Spirit. Read the sources: John 3:8 (World English Bible) · Ezekiel 37:1–14, Hebrew and English (Mechon Mamre) · Mounce: Greek headword Back to the term index ↑

term-prince-of-life.name: Prince of Life
term-prince-of-life.text: Jesus Christ · Greek: ἀρχηγός (archēgos) A title of Jesus in Acts 3:15 (KJV: “Prince of life”), where Peter contrasts his death with God’s raising him from the dead. Archēgos can denote a leader or originator; here “prince” does not simply mean a king’s son. The title concerns Jesus’ relationship to life. Read it within Peter’s appeal to his hearers, not as collective blame against Jewish people across history. This Greek word differs from archōn , the word for ruler in the hostile titles below. Read the sources: Acts 3:12–26 (KJV) · Acts 3:15: Greek text and parsing · Thayer: archēgos · Related Son-title study Back to the term index ↑

term-prince-of-peace.name: Prince of Peace
term-prince-of-peace.text: Biblical royal title, applied to Jesus in Christian interpretation · Hebrew: שַׂר־שָׁלוֹם (śar-šālôm) Isaiah 9:6 (KJV) includes “The Prince of Peace” among the promised child’s royal titles. The following verse connects his rule with David’s throne, justice, righteousness, and enduring peace. The Hebrew joins śar , ruler or commander, with šālôm , peace and well-being. Christian interpretation applies this passage to Jesus; interpretation of its original royal setting differs. Edition distinction: Brenton’s Septuagint translation of Isaiah 9:6 instead calls the child “the Messenger of great counsel.” “Prince of Peace” is therefore indexed here as Hebrew-based wording, not quoted as Brenton’s

term-prince-of-the-power-of-the-air.name: Prince of the Power of the Air
term-prince-of-the-power-of-the-air.text: Adversarial title, traditionally identified with Satan · Shortened search alias: Prince of the Air The full KJV wording in Ephesians 2:2 is “the prince of the power of the air.” “Prince of the Air” is a shortened alias, not an exact quotation of that verse. The Greek combines ἄρχων ( archōn , ruler), ἐξουσία ( exousia , authority or power), and ἀήρ ( aēr , air). The passage describes a hostile spiritual ruler associated with disobedience, traditionally understood as Satan, before contrasting the former sinful life with God’s mercy in Christ. It does not identify Jesus or justify assigning the title to modern broadcasting or technology. Read the sources: Ephesians 2:1–10 (KJV) · Ephesians 2:2

term-prince-of-this-world.name: Prince of This World
term-prince-of-this-world.text: Adversarial title, traditionally identified with Satan · Greek: ἄρχων (archōn), ruler John 12:31, 14:30, and 16:11 use this designation (KJV: “the prince of this world”) for the hostile ruler traditionally identified as Satan. The passages emphasize his limits and defeat: he is to be cast out, has no claim upon Jesus, and stands judged. These verses use a title rather than the personal name Satan. This is not a title of Jesus, nor does it place the adversary on an equal footing with God. The referent and context, not the shared English word “prince,” determine the meaning. Read the sources: John 12:31: Greek and KJV · John 14:30 (KJV) · John 16:11 (KJV) · Thayer: archōn · Related spiritual-o

term-savor.name: Savor / Savour
term-savor.text: English spelling variants · KJV examples use “savour” and “savourest” · Several distinct underlying words An older English word whose meaning must be read in context. Keep these uses distinct rather than treating them as one original-language lemma: Taste: in Matthew 5:13, salt losing its “savour” means losing its saltiness. The Greek verb μωραίνω ( mōrainō ) is used here of becoming tasteless; “savour” is part of the English rendering, not a separate Greek noun in this clause. Aroma: in 2 Corinthians 2:14–16, “savour” belongs to Paul’s imagery of fragrance and its differing reception. Greek ὀσμή ( osmē , verses 14 and 16) denotes smell or odor, while εὐωδία ( euōdia , verse 15) denotes frag

term-selah.name: Selah
term-selah.text: Hebrew term retained in many translations · Precise meaning uncertain A term found within the Psalms and the prayer in Habakkuk 3. Psalm 3 in the World English Bible Classic places Selah after verses 2, 4, and 8. The New American Bible, Revised Edition numbers the corresponding lines 3, 5, and 9 because its superscription is numbered as verse 1. The NABRE note describes Selah as generally understood to be an instruction for singers or musicians, while acknowledging that its exact meaning is unknown. A pause or musical cue is a proposal, not an established translation of “stop and think.” Pausing for reflection can be a useful reading practice, but should be identified as a devotional applica

term-septuagint.name: Septuagint / LXX
term-septuagint.text: Greek biblical textual tradition · LXX = seventy A name used for the ancient Greek Scriptures associated with the translation and transmission of Israel’s sacred writings. LXX, the Roman numeral for seventy, recalls a traditional account of their translation. The collection has a complex textual history: its books should not be treated as one uniform translation produced in a single sitting. Read the sources: Greek Orthodox Archdiocese and Hellenic Bible Society: About Septuagint.Bible · IOSCS: commentary prospectus, especially the anthology distinction Back to the term index ↑

term-soteriology.name: Soteriology
term-soteriology.text: Later theological study terminology · The study of salvation In Christian theology, soteriology names the study of salvation, including questions about Christ’s saving work, grace, faith, justification, and growth in holiness. It is a label for a field of study, not a quotation from a biblical verse. Glenn Kreider’s Dallas Theological Seminary course introduction illustrates this usage and explicitly includes sanctification within its wider scope. Begin with passages before comparing theological systems. Ephesians 2:8–10 speaks of salvation as God’s gift received through faith and of a life prepared for good works. Soteriology asks how passages like this relate to the wider biblical witness;

term-targum.name: Targum / Targumim
term-targum.text: Jewish Aramaic translation and interpretation · Plural: targumim In biblical study, targum commonly refers to an Aramaic version of a biblical book; the word also carries the sense of translation or interpretation. The targumim are distinct works, not one uniform translation. When a study cites “the Targum,” ask which work, passage and edition it means. Manchester’s trilingual Bible catalogue identifies Targum Onkelos alongside the Pentateuch and Targum Jonathan alongside the prophetic readings. It separately identifies Saʿadia Gaon’s Tafsir as Judeo-Arabic: that is not another Aramaic targum. These distinctions help prevent different languages and works from being merged under a single labe

term-theosis.name: Theosis
term-theosis.text: Eastern Orthodox theological usage In Eastern Orthodox theology, theosis names participation in God’s life through Christ and the Holy Spirit, often described as deification. It concerns transformation by grace, expressed in holiness and love. This entry describes Orthodox usage; its theological framework should not be assumed to be identical to every other Christian account of salvation. Read the sources: Orthodox Church in America: The Holy Trinity in Christian Life · Orthodox Church in America: Ascension, including 2 Peter 1:4 Back to the term index ↑

term-trinity.name: Trinity
term-trinity.text: Trinitarian Christian doctrine In Trinitarian Christian theology, God is one in divine being and three in persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The persons are genuinely distinct, without constituting three gods. The Catholic source cited here explains this doctrinal formulation; Christian groups that reject the Trinity understand these relationships differently. Read the sources: Catholic formulation: Catechism §§249–255 Back to the term index ↑

term-vulgate.name: Vulgate
term-vulgate.text: Latin edition title: Biblia Sacra Vulgata The Latin biblical tradition associated especially with Jerome’s work of translation and revision in late antiquity. It deeply influenced Western Christian worship, theology, and language. When consulting a Vulgate, identify the edition: a modern critical text such as Weber–Gryson and the Catholic Church’s Nova Vulgata have different editorial histories and purposes. Read the sources: German Bible Society: Biblia Sacra Vulgata edition description · Francis: Scripturae Sacrae affectus, section “The Vulgate” Back to the term index ↑

term-wesleyan-quadrilateral.name: Wesleyan Quadrilateral
term-wesleyan-quadrilateral.text: Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience · Wesleyan theological reflection The Wesleyan Quadrilateral describes four resources used in Wesleyan theological reflection: Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience. The name is a later description of John Wesley’s approach; Wesley did not formulate a method under that title. In United Methodist teaching, Scripture is the primary source and standard for Christian doctrine. The four resources therefore have distinct roles, rather than equal authority. United Methodist glossary Scripture: Study the biblical witness carefully, attending to context and the whole Bible. Tradition: Listen to the Church’s inherited teaching, worship, and interpret

word-study.name: Read the word in context
word-study.text: Begin with the passage. Read the whole sentence and its surrounding argument or story before choosing a meaning. Identify the word and its form. A dictionary headword is a starting point; tense, case, syntax, and context can matter. Compare actual uses. A word’s history or parts do not determine every later use. Several possible senses do not all apply at once. Distinguish language from interpretation. A lexical observation, a theological conclusion, and a later church formulation are related kinds of study, but require different evidence.

sources.name: About these sources
sources.text: Scripture links identify a specific passage, even when the destination opens at a chapter. Language aids document headwords and usage; they are not interchangeable with a critical text or apparatus. Official church texts are cited as statements of the named tradition, rather than as evidence that every Christian community uses a term identically. Greek, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Latin appear where relevant. The Latin Vulgate belongs to the Bible’s translation and reception history; it is not the original language of the New Testament.
